speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

Mr. Speaker, by your leave may I be permitted to read a telegram which I have just received, and which has been sent to me in order to correct a statement which was made a few days ago by the hon. member for DuffeTin (Mr. Best), with regard to contributions made in Montreal by the French Canadian people in connection with the war. The telegram is as follows:
Montreal, January 29, 1917.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier,
Ottawa.
As chairman of day's pay Committee which last year secured subscriptions exceeding five hundred thousand dollars from employees in Montreal, I can safely say that at least half of this amount was contributed by French-Cana-dian workingmen and women. The English and French-Canadian citizens of Montreal are at present working hand in hand in the organization of another campaign to raise two and a half million dollars here in February. All interests are working together in the most energetic and harmonious manner for its success.
J. W. McConnell.

(Resuming.) Mr. Speaker, when the debate adjourned last night I was saying that I believed it was the duty of every man in this House and every man in public life in this country to work for the harmony of the races which compose the people of Canada. I was speaking of the attacks which have been made upon the province of Quebec, and of attacks which have been especially directed

against the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). I spoke also of the testimony which had been given at the banquet in the city of Vancouver by the late hon. the Postmaster General, Mr. T. C. Casgrain, when he said that there was no anti-war feeling in the province of Quebec, and that he could testify that at the very outset of the struggle my right hon. friend and others oh this side of the House had laid aside their political opinions and had appeared with him upon the public platform of that province to advocate recruiting. I could have gone further and instanced testimonials of loyalty which were given to my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition at different banquets in the city of London, notably at the banquet at the Imperial Institute in June, 1897, which was presided over by the then Prince of Wales, afterwards King Edward VII. I do not think that it is absolutely necessary this afternoon to do so, and I shall content myself simply with stating, in answer to hon. gentlemen opposite, that one of the present ministers, the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Sevigny), speaking in the county of Dorchester
Hear, hear.

That "hear, hear" is very weak. However, we will let that pass. Here is what Mr. Sevigny said:
After explaining National Service as usual, Mr. Sevigny said that he was ready to retire and leave the field to Mr. -Cannon if anybody present was ready to say that Sir Wilfrid Laurier had not advised the people to sign the National -Service cards.
Sir, I give that testimony to the House for what it may be worth.
The second thought that was in my mind, and with that I shall conclude my remarks this afternoon, was the attempt which is being made by gentlemen opposite to make political capital out of this war so as to satisfy the prejudice of political opinion. We have had instances of that in this country unfortunately, both in the public press and in the utterances of men in public life. I did tell you last night, that when the right hon. leader of the Opposition was in the province of Quebec urging the young men to join the colours, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers) was out in the town of Aylmer trying to incite his friends to find somebody in the county of Wright who would redeem it to the Conservative cause. Let me instance another case. The whole province of Ontario, and in fact the Dominion of Canada, was thrilled by the words

of Mr. Ralph Connor in the city of Toronto calling upon the people of this country for national unity and saying that there was only one thing worth while, and that was winning the struggle. Yet the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) sat back and contented himself with dismissing the idea by saying: "Well, Ralph Connor, after all, is only ,a Grit." Now, Sir, we have other gentlemen who have the honour of having seats on the treasury benches who are trying to make political capital out of the war-Let me begin with the right hon. gentleman who leads this Government. The House was amazed and the country was amazed the other night when the right hon. gentleman who, generally speaking, has the reputation of being broad-minded, thought it necessary to cast aspersions on the right hon. 'leader of the Opposition for some attitude, which he did not thoroughly explain, mark well, but which would give the impression to friends opposite and to others in the country that Sir Wilfrid Laurier was disloyal to the Empire during the South African war, when the history of the case, when all the facts of the case, are directly against such a contention. Is it surprising, then, that other members of his Cabinet stoop so low as to- try and make political capital out of the war. We have the -hon. Minister of-What is he now? He is Postmaster General, Mr. Blondin. Speaking in the county of Dorchester a few days ago, and what was he doing in the county of Dorchester? Was he advocating recruiting?
Oh, oh; it hurts.

It hurts? I have no doubt it does hurt hon. gentlemen opposite. What was the Postmaster General saying in the . county of Dorchester? Does it cause merriment upon the other side? It did not cause as much merriment with the right thinking people of Canada after they had read the words which were uttered by the Postmaster General. He was not advocating recruiting, but a policy of emigration from this country to the United States.
Oh, oh, "take it back"; "that's exploded."

Let me give his words; I am quoting now from the Montreal Gazette of January 26:
St. Germaine, Dorchester County, Quebec, January 25th:	The following affidavit was
given out to-n'ght by the Liberal chiefs here:
We, the undersigned, declare that we heard last night at Ste. Rose, January 24, 1917, the Hon. P. E: Blondin make the following declara-

tion:	"As for the Allison scandal and others
of the same nature, let us suppose that if these thefts have taken place, It has no importance for the people of Ste. Rose, because it was English money that was stolen."
Speaking of the danger of conscription, Mr. Blondin declared that, even if conscription was put into force, that would mean little to the people of Ste. Rose, because they had only to go across the frontier to get away.
That language was intended for home consumption, but when he found that these words had gone abroad, Mr. Blondin thought he would manufacture something else; so he immediately sent a correction, and I take his correction from the Ottawa Evening Journal, another good Tory paper. Here is what he says:
The statement which has been sworn to by certain Liberals with regard to my utterances are a distortion of my words. I never by any means intended to convey-
Mark well, that he did not intend to convey.
-the meaning which they have attached to my speech.
So it was not plain speaking.
Mr. Cannon had been stating in his speeches that the Conservative party had been grafting from the Canadian treasury in connection with munition contracts.
No man in this House or in the country can deny that.
In my speech at Ste. Rose I explained that it was not true that the Allison scandal had to do with Canadian money, pointing out that the money paid for the shells was the money of the British Government.
It was all right to steal the money because it came from the British Government; it would have been a crime if the money had come from the Canadian Government.
In regard to the conscription matter I told the people of Ste. Rose that I did not believe conscription would be necessary because so many Canadians were eager to go and fight for the cause of liberty and humanity. I added chat if any of them were afraid of conscription, if conscription should be passed and they did not want to go to the war, they had a remedy left. They could go across the United States line which is near Ste. Rose and escape military service.
Will hon. gentlemen opposite now applaud these words? There was another statement made by the hon. gentleman, only it was for exportation. It is contained in the wire which he sent to the right hon. gentleman, the Prime Minister, on the morning of the election. Mark well, for therein lies the danger. Here is an hon. gentleman in the Cabinet who makes a statement sworn to by electors of this
country. He finds that that statement is creating disturbance in the Conservative ranks, and he makes a correction which is worse than the original statement. Then he lets matters go on until the morning uf the election when he sends a telegram to the Prime Minister in which he does not refer to his words upon conscription. I hold a copy of the telegram in my hand, and not a word in it refers to conscription. He does not deny that he advised the people of Dorchester County to go across the line to the United States. And yet hon. gentlemen opposite say that they are not making political capital out of the war.
Let me say to my hon. friends opposite that their press, backed by the party, is creating the same sentiment in this country as that to which I have referred. The chief organ of the Conservative Party in the province of Quebec is L'Evenement, and here is a sample of what that paper was publishing during the Dorchester campaign. I quote it for the sake of my merry friends opposite:
I may first state, however, that the idea of L'Evenement was this:	If conscription
was adopted in Canada it would not be due to any action on the part of the Conservative party; the sole blame was to fall on the head of my right hon. friend who leads the Opposition. L'Evenement prints in very large type for distribution throughout the county of Dorchester words that were signed by my right hon. friend's friend of 1911, Mr. Henri Bourassa, the friend of the Postmaster General of the present day (Mr. Blondin), of the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Sevigny), and of the Secretary of State (Mr. Patenaude). The statement published in L'Evenement is as follows:
If England were, I will not say in danger, but simply at grips with one or two or several of the great powers of Europe, the Prime Minister could demand not $35,00'0,000, but two, three, or four times $35,000,0'0I0, We would put all the resources of Canada at the disposal of England. There would not be a single discordant voice.
These words were not given to the electors of Dorchester county as those of the Prime Minister of this country; they were given as the words lately uttered by the right hon. the leader of the Opposition. Again in big type, we find this in L'Evenement:
It was Sir Wilfrid Laurier who had passed in 1904 the Militia Act which would permit of the establishment of conscription in Canada. This Act is found in Chapter 41 of the Statutes of Canada of 1906.
And the article ends:

If we shall ever have conscription, it would be put into force thanks to a law passed by Laurier. Electors of Dorchester do not forget that.
I submit, Sir, that the Government have been making all the political capital possible out of this war. The Prime Minister made a statement and gave figures, which I quoted last night, purporting to show just what the Government had done for the Allied cause. He took credit to himself for having sent a large number of young men across the ocean. He stated that he had sent some 17,000 Russian, Italian, and French reservists. I want to tell my right hon. friend that if he or his Government had never existed, and the war went on, those French, Russian and Italian reservists would have had to go anyway under the laws of the countries whence they came.
I ask my hon. friend if he is in favour of conscription under any circumstances?
Will it materially aid my hon. friend if I enter into a dissertation upon conscription? The question will come up in the House when it will be discussed fully.	[DOT]
Oh, oh.

At the proper time, I will give my views upon the question of conscription, and I will be very happy to listen to my hon. friend when he gives his views. But I assure my hon. friend, that if I had to go to fight I would go to fight, and would not come back to Canada unless I came back wounded.
You evidently won't go at all.

firm then. Do not trust the Grits." Then comes quite an extract from a communication to me:
Now is your chance to get even with the * inance Minister and the High Commissioner, or Overseas Minister of Militia, for their intrigue and undermining you. Can't you see the ring against you? The Montreal Daily Mail, the Montreal Evening News (both owned by a half brother of the Finance Minister), the Toronto Telegram, on which the Finance Minister served for years and which is regarded as his Toronto organ, whose editor is reported about to be knighted for viciously attacking vou ; whose representative and nephew in London. connected by marriage with the High Commissioner, or Overseas Minister of Militia, has been constant in misrepresenting you, and slobbering over your enemies in the Associated Press notices from England, paid for by Canadian money-these Tory papers and people have led in the vicious attacks on, and attempts to undermine you.
And he writes a lot more that I will not read. Even the dear old Toronto Globe gives advice and warning against the Tory pitfalls, and the Ottawa Journal-Press urges me to beware of the wily old politician from Quebec, under whom the editor of that paper so long served. It is very pleasing to receive such good advice. But some of those now urging me to stand to my friends were, within a year, active in urging me to desert friends as true, as honourable, as capable, as patriotic, as self-sacrificing, men who have done as much for the cause of humanity and the Allies in this war, as could be done; while others now professing friendship and offering advice were then busy in their efforts to discredit me. All good advice, but Sam Hughes now, as then, stands by principles and by every honourable man, rather than in wasting his time attacking mere creatures of the hour. Men are transient and soon forgotten, but principles are eternal.
Many people-and I am sorry to see by reading the Hansard debates, even some members of this House-seem .to forget that we are engaged in a struggle for our very existence. Now, Sir, I am a firm believer in responsible government, which means party government. I always waive non-essentials for party, but always as certainly do I waive party for essentials. With me, country and cause come first. I have differed from party leaders in days' gpne by, but the verdict of history has vindicated my action in every instance. Party government involves intelligence, instruction, and independence on the part of the electorate. Party government involves the same conditions for members of Parliament, and let me also say, party government involves the same conditions for a
[Sir Sam Hughes I
cabinet. Party government does not imply autocracy either in the leader or in the cabinet. The danger of party government is where members lose their independence for any cause-for hope of .office, or reward, or for any other reason sacrifice their individuality for temporary, selfish and incompetent leaders. IThe party should always assert itself; its members should not be mere slavish followers.
Now, as to loyalty. My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has claimed that it is a vice or a weakness in me that my heart gets the better of my head. I have studied history and have observed that no man has ever benefited humanity whose heart did not greatly overbalance his head. But there is not much danger in some quarters of any such over-balancing. My way is not strewn with milestones to abandoned friends. The Prime Minister has stated that he has always been loyal to his colleagues, and his colleagues have been and are loyal to him. I think it is quite unnecessary that I should take up the time of this House for a single moment in reviewing my loyalty to the Prime Minister of Canada, but it might be not amiss to inform the public and the House that Canada and Great Britain are engaged in a war to the death, and that I shall stand by party where party interests are the people's and the soldiers' interests-but, where the party fails in its duty, especially in regard to the war and to our soldiers, then I shall not hesitate to have duty done and self-sacrificing patriotism rewarded.
I am strongly urged by some to stand true to my friends. Why, the reproach to me by many is that I never desert a friend. I may be deserted; but to break with the dear good fellows of the great Liberal-Conservative party would wrench me almost as much as losing the war. It pains me to see, however, that party feelings, party prejudices, are so strong in Canada over non-essentials.
I have been asked by some-not officially by Liberal leaders; I want to make that distinctly understood-to cast in my lot with Laurier and the great, time-honoured Liberal party. In all love and kindness, let me say that the idea shocked me. To assist in placing a statesman of even his high character and power, with the principles enunciated by his authorised supporter in Dorchester, and have Canada depend on his ideals for the conduct and the

settlement of the war, would be repugnant to my very soul, although everyone knows my personal admiration for the right hon. leader of the Opposition.
"Canada has done enough in this war for England." and sn forth, are the utterances of the acknowledged, the endorsed henchmen of the right hon. leader of the Opposition. Canada is forced into this war, not for or by Britain; for Britain never asked a man, never hinted for a man; but Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific sprang to arms because the liberties of this fair land were and still are threatened.
Whatever my course to-day may be, and whatever the effect to me may be, you may rest assured, Sir, that my aim, my purpose, my determination, has but one conclusion: the active, energetic conduct of the war to a victorious issue. Men and munitions, and still more men and more munitions, is the cry. Our hearts go out to the gallant boys at the front, and also to their mothers and other loved ones at home who long for the return of the lads; or if they be not among those returning, to get a chance some time to see the spot where the beloved boy did his duty and gave his life for human liberty and dear old down-trodden humanity. These people, as well as our soldiers themselves, ask, what is Canada doing? Canada has a higher duty to perform, a more important duty in the war, than gathering harvests, assisting in making munitions and helping to furnish bread to the soldiers. And yet, as reported by the Montreal Gazette and the Ottawa Journal-Press, the hon. Mr. Sevigny, in a speech delivered -by him, stated that the only duty of Canada was to gather harvests, assist in making munitions and help to furnish bread to the soldiers. I have no hesitation in saying that I think the right hon. leader of the Opposition, unless he could prove that his candidate in Dorchester had not uttered the words he did, should have called him off in that contest or repudiated him publicly, and I have also no hesitation in saying that the right hon. leader of the Government, when he read these words uttered by Mr. Sevigny and when he read the speech delivered by Mr. Blondin, should have, without any delay, repudiated those gentlemen or called for a cancellation of their statements. I wonder why the good people of Dorchester county did not throw both candidates out of their riding, if the piffle we hear was really uttered amongst them. I have always claimed that the
people of the province of Quebec have never had a real opportunity of showing what they can do. They have had this party and that party. In 1896 it was the Liberal party, with the cry: What, going to put Tupper in and spend three million dollars to send your sons off to fight? A few years later it was the Conservative party going through the ridings of the province and proclaiming the same sort of doctrine, appealing to the passions and prejudices of the people. My experience of the people of the province of Quebec is that, when they hear the proper side of a case, they act like men, and when they get an opportunity to go to the front and fight, they fight like men; and it annoys and maddens me to see the two great parties of the Canadian people tell -them all that little tittle-tattle that was reported in the papers in connection with the Dorchester election.
Argentine and the United States both supply harvests and make munitions and furnish bread for our soldiers. Canada should do a little more. WThat action is being carried on by Canada? We must go forward and not backward. Let action be the mandate.
It is well known to the members of this House and the people of this country that my policy has been for many a long year and still stronger is than ever before: Full partnership of Great Britain and her colonies throughout the world, with the great Central Government dealing with what concerns the Empire, and each of the component parts of the Empire dealing with what concerns itself in various degrees, and one not interfering with the other. Therefore, any stand which I may take to-day for the protection of our Canadian soldiers at the front, for the up-building of our army, and for the success o' the cause, will, you may rest assured, be along the lines of my love and admiration for all that is great and good in the motherland, but the motherland should take her own -position in relation to her soldiers, and Canada should have absolute control of her soldiers.	,
In the addresses of both the right hon. leader of the Opposition and the right hon. leader of the Government reference was made to participation by Canada in the South African war. May I be permitted to mention one or two particulars in that connection? Let me frankly say that I was the one who had the honour of first bringing up this subject in the Parliament of Canada, and I was brow-beaten by my honoured

I desire to place on Hansard notes 2, 3, 4, and 5, relating to section 177, as follows:
(2)	This section applies to what may be termed strictly colonial forces, that is to say, forces raised on the responsibility of the government of the colony. The amendments made by A. A. A., 1909 and 1912 are intended to make it clear that colonial legislatures can apply the

whole of the Army Act, or any part of it, to the
forces of the colony, subject to such adaptations as may he necessary to make them applicable.
(3)	So long as such forces are within the colony their discipline can be provided for by the law of the colony. This section removes any doubts as to whether that law would apply to such forces when outside the limits of the colony.
(4)	In order to prevent difficulties arising from deficiencies of the colonial law in cases where the colonial forces are serving with the regular forces, the section provides that such deficiencies may be remedied by the application of the Army Act, subject to any modification made by general orders of the general officer commanding the regular forces in question.
(5)	"This section shall not apply", etc. The effect of this provision (added by A. A. A., 1909) is that where the Army Act applies to colonial forces serving with the regulars (see, for instance s. 175 (11) and s. 176 (8. A.), it will apply to them as if they were regulars.
Then there is axi explanatory clause:
The last paragraph of section 177 beginning "this section shall not apply," etc., had also in view, when it was added, the control of bodies of militia or troops from the colonies visiting the United Kingdom.
My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition will remember this because it was passed when he was Prime Minister. He may remember that soldiers went over to Britain for athletic purposes, or to the Coronation, or for some other purpose, and they went around England in uniform without any control; and this clause was added: Then in regard to colonial forces, Class 2, not only are colonial forces, Class 1, undeT colonial law in any part of the world, but colonial forces, Class 2 are exempted from the Army Act where a Colonial Act is in existence applying thereto. Now, Sir, I wish to take up the question of service under the Militia Act. At the time of the census of 1911 the male population of Canada between the ages of 18 years and 45 years, was 1,720,000. Married men in Canada of all ages numbered
1,332,000,	and married men over 45 years of age numbered 650,000. The number of married men under 45 years of age was estimated at 682,000. Duduct from the total of 1,720,000 the 682,000 men, and you have 1,088,000 single men in Canada between 18 years of age and 45 years of age. The number already enrolled is 400,000,
100,000	married men and 300,000 single men. Therefore according to the census of seven years ago, there are 788,000 single men in Canada, who have not enlisted. We can apply the Militia Act and get for home training and defence, any number we like, say, 300,000 men. Then in the spring we could call fpr volunteers for overseas, and I am satisfied that there is not a district in Canada that would not furnish its quota. If we did not get enough volunteers for overseas we could send them under the law as militia, each district being credited with the men already enrolled therefrom. Here let me point out what I found in the course of my visits to Quebec. One gentleman would say:	why should my
sons go away to the front and perhaps be maimed for life if my neighbour does not allow his sons to go. There was one case of a gentleman who had four sons. They wanted to go, but he would not let them. He asked whether it was fair that he should let them go and run the chance of becoming maimed for ilijfe while the fellows who went into the munition factories remained at home and earned their $4, $5 and $6 a day. We are all human, and there is a good deal of logic in the position taken by that man. I am satisfied that you would meet the wishes of the great mass of people of the province of Quebec, as well as of every other part of the Dominion, by applying the Militia Act and by siaying:	"We will take so many
men for home defence, and then when we
want more soldiers to go overseas we will call for volunteers. If there are not enough, we will send them under the Militia Act." I am satisfied that these men would do their duty fearlessly and well.
The rule from time immemorial in Britain has been that the man becoming a soldier loses no rights of citizenship. On the contrary, special privileges have been conferred upon him as a soldier. I may point out that while in England last summer, the question arose as to the right of the soldiers of British Columbia to vote in the provincial election. Those I talked to were men high up; they were not underlings. I asked them what right they had to refuse permission to the soldiers of British Columbia to vote. I asked under what authority they meddled. I pointed out that the province of British Columbia was a self-governing province and that Canada was a self-governing country, and that if British Columbia wanted her soldiers to vote all she had to do was to notify the Prime Minister of Canada and he would arrange the matter through whatever diplomatic channel he chose. I quoted, also, that the rule from time immemorial in Britain was that the man, in becoming a soldier, loses no right of citizenship, but that on the contrary special privileges have been conferred upon him as such soldier. I fail to see why the soldier at the front should be disfranchised, while the slacker or the munition worker at home should exercise his franchise. The Home Government appoints the Governor General of Canada; Canada has the right of appeal to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. The command in chief of Canadian forces rests with His Majesty through the Governor General, which, of course, means through the Governor General in Council. Thus Canada hae absolute control of her soldiers in Canada, in the United Kingdom, and at the front, subject to any general order of the Commander in Chief, but such order must be in conformity with the laws of Canada and subject thereto. Canada, therefore, has the absolute right to provide her own equipment, arms, ammunition, supplies, transport; in short, everything for her troops at the front. Further, the appointment and promotion of officers rests entirely with Canada for her troops in any part of the world. Any association with the War Office in any of these regards is merely a matter of convenience, courtesy, and for exchange

of ideas. The Canadian forces are in no sense British regulars. The wisdom and foresight of British statesmen and War Office officials in framing the Army Act and amendments .thereto have left nothing unguarded in the interests of the colonies. Where the practice has differed from the law the fault lies with those concerned for not understanding, or, if understanding, for not applying the law. It was'different in the case of the contingents we sent to South Africa. There Britain paid while Canada, as agent of Britain, enrolled. Now, Canada as Canada, not as an agent, enrolls, pays and controls. I am not casting that up as any reflection upon the ex-Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). I may say here that the plan to be followed in relation to our Canadian troops was laid down by me with Lord Lansdowne two years before the South African war broke out. Lord Lansdowne has the plans which I laid down in the month of December, 1897, for colonial assistance before war broke out, and the Sydney Daily Telegraph, an Australian newspaper, on the occasion of my visit there in 1897, published a statement exactly bearing out the line of policy I had laid down.
I see some of my Liberal friends opposite looking as if they thought that I was finding fault. I am responsible for the plan that was carried out. In view of the opposition there was in Canada and in other parts of the world to the colonies serving for the Motherland, I thought the best plan would be .at the start to let the troops be paid by Britain and thus one objection would be removed. I had taken the matter up previously with Lord Lansdowne and the identical plan that I propo.sed was the one that was carried out. Canada furnishes her own uniforms, weapons, equipment, hospitals, nurses, and doctors' staff, and yet, when I sent over the dentists, the first time the system had ever been introduced, they were thrown out by the medical service of Great Britain and attached to the British hospitals up and down the line; they would not have them. We put our foot down and finally, after a great deal of struggling, they were recognized. They were to have one dentist with every hospital. They were bound that the dentists 'should be under the control of the medical officers, and I was bound, that they should not be. I did not see why a dentist who was over twenty-one years of age should not be allowed to pull a tooth without having to do it under the authority of a medical officer.
I take the ground that it is none of the business of Great Britain if we chose to. use wheel-harrows for our transport service at the front. We must take it for granted that we know our business and that Canada will have the best things that are going as we have the best things that are going, and that it is our privilege to say what is good and what is no good. In this connection the Prime Minister made a .statement the other night and the ground which be took then is the gfound which has been taken by others. In bringing this up I am not divulging any secret. Without actually quoting the right hon. gentleman, he said that wherever a committee of the British service examined goods and threw them out he was ready to abide by the decision of that committee. That, I think, is a fair interpretation of the right hon. gentleman's remarks.

On the other hand, I do not propose, I have not proposed in the past, and I do not propose in the future to set up my judgment or the judgment of this Government against the opinion of military experts who may say that it is necessary that the type of equipment, of transport, or of anything else necessary in this war ought to he uniform and that the war cannot he carried on effectively unless it is uniform.
That is the ground taken by the Prime MiniisteT. I am not finding the slightest fault with his taking that ground, but it is not the ground I take. The halo had gone off a lot of these fellows so far as I was concerned long ago, and I did not see why the opinion of a young sprig of a captain about twenty-two years of age, who threw out our equipment should prevail as against the opinion of a young Canadian officer. I am not impressed with any man who shuts out any Canadian stuff, such, for instance, as our Canadian wagons. Our little Canadian, two-horse wagons ini South Africa would carry a heavier load than the British wagons with four teams1, and we could out-distance and out-travel them. In the Northwest Rebellion the ordinary farm wagons which were used there travelled more miles up to their axles, in mud than the heavy British wagons travelled on the good roads of France and Belgium. But, let us see for a moment how these inspections are made and what they amount to- Here is a letter that was addressed to me as Minister of Militia:

Re Motor Lorries:
The main fault that the Mechanical Transport Department of the War Office had to find with our Motor Lorries was the fact that we had five makes in use, three of which were being sent over to Prance, and which necessitated carrying over spare parts for all these various makes.
When I heard that everything else had been thrown out, I naturally raised Cain with my .officers here and found that everything was all right.
As I advised you before, when our 1st Division were ready to go to France, the British Mechanical Transport Department supplied us with 51 motor lorries and 9 motor cars to make our equipment complete.
The motors they rejected cost us about $2,800 each, and they charged for the ones they gave us $5,241 apiece.
I have been endeavouring ever since I got back here to get details of these lorries and cars; these have just been received by me and I am more than astonished to find that six English makes of motor lorries were supplied

These people do beat me! They impressed on me in no uncertain terms that we must positively get down our makes of motor lorries to if possible two, as the question of taking spare parts to the Continent and keeping them in stock was a very serious one indeed, and here they are doing the very thing that we were instructed not to do and doing it to a much greater extent than we had ever dreamt of doing. These things are rather difficult for me to comprehend, and X intend to take the matter up with the War Office officially tomorrow, but do not expect that I shall receive any more satisfaction than usual.
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd) John W. Carson. So that the claim was all moonshine that we must have a uniform system in regard
to the trucks because they themselves had nothing of the kind.
I take the stand that the soldiers who fought and won at St. Julien, Festubert, etc., are fit to furnish soldiers and officers for any service, and that we have inspectors in Canada who can determine what we shall have and what we shall not have. I did not know there were any people in the universe who would revive that old, exploded idea, but to show that there are such pre-historic people, I may say that the auditor general on his return recently brought back the old question which I explained last year, as to why our transport wagons and that sort of thing had been thrown out. I do not want to repeat what I have already said, but I may say that the objection to our wagons was based chiefly on the ground that they could not turn on the narrow roads of France. Why, Sir, the British wagon takes 35 feet of a circle in which to turn, while purs takes 31 feet 9 inches. That was put before the Government in May 1915, or earlier, and yet we find a British officer in our service here bringing it up again a short time ago. The thing is nonsense. Our wagon turns in 31 feet 9 inches, while theirs takes 35 feet and, as I have already pointed out, our wagon has proved better and has outlasted theirs. My stand is that Canada should decide as to what she herself shall use.
Before my hon. friend leaves that matter, could he say what was the value of the equipment which was thrown away?

I forget; it was millions. We did not look at the value; we were so busy" swearing we had no time to figure up the value. Now, Mr. Speaker, my Object in bringing this matter up is this: I am anxious that this Empire shall rest upon a stable foundation. I have given the best years of my life to advocating the cause of full partnership union. I have taken part in two wars for the Empire, and I am going to stand or fall by the rights of Canada under its Constitution.
In the first year of the war Canada had no say whatever. In the appointment of General Carson to go over there and represent me, I -brought in my Order in Council. My idea was that he should represent the minister over there, and look after the soldiers' interests, and things of that kind, but he was only allowed to look after -supplies. I -am ' not blaming anybody; this is not a new thing. I had the same trouble in South Africa, where it was pointed out

that the British did the paying, and I did some very vigorous kicking at that time on the rights of Canadians. In this war we are doing the paying, the equipping and outfitting of our men, and the ground I take is not in the interests of Canada alone, but in the interests of the whole Empire, because unless we have a proper understanding things are going to go wrong. Why, at the very time I have been speaking of, when these motor trucks were being purchased, every man that came home invalided, and every letter from the front, talked of another Boston tea party. It went so far that some fellows on the staff drew 'lots as to who should punch the head of -the officer who -had been offensive to them. Can I he blamed for standing to the law? Carson was n-ot to interfere in any way with the forces. The Pay Department was modelled after the British, and so was the medical service.
Now, my hon. friends opposite cannot make any political capital out of this, for it is the same with Grit and Tory alike. Today, in Great Britain, you appoint a Canadian to an office and when a British officer comes along the Canadian kow-tows to him. That is the only fault I have to find with Canadians in Great Britain. They have not understood their individuality as Canadians, and have not stood up for their rights kind-ly -and firmly. The only Canadian officer who has done it to ithe King's- taste is Frank Meighen of Montreal. He has -stood up for the rights of Canada under the law up to the hilt and he gets along better than any other officer in our force.
I am not going to enter into- -a discussion of the medical service to-day, -but rest assured that when- the time comes I -shal-1 have a hand in- it, and -it may be, up to- the elbow. Last year when I was in the Old Country I found that under Colonel Jones' administration

and the Prime Minister will remember this-it took me three weeks to get from -him a list of the hospitals scattered all over the country in which our men were being treated. I asked at the time why, when we were paying the expenses of our own men, they should be treated in V.A.D. hospitals away up in the north of England -and other parts of the United Kingdom, and I -asked why ou-r good nurses with three years' training were being utilized for more than half their time looking after British soldiers. I -asked why when we were paying seventy-five cents a day, we should have our fel-low-s' brows smoothed -and -their bands held by nice little gir-ls w-ho had taken a six weeks' course in the

St. John's Ambu-anee Corps or -something like -that. It was very congenial of course, but -at the same time I think our boyis would have liked to have their brows smoothed and their hands held by our o-wn girls.
As to the command of the troops, I have recognized from the outset th-at in the field the troops should be, not that they legally -are, under the command of -a British officer. The general command of the troops is part of the law, -and I have n-ot sought to evade the law in- the slightest degree. When it came to sending over the second division- and the Prime Minister disputed my statement the other night, that I had informed him in regard to this and I might here remind him that I showed him copies of my telegram to Lord Kitchener, -and the Prime Minister drew my attention to -the -fact that in one of the telegrams my language was a little too strong. In other words, I received a gentle reprimand for my language in one of the telegrams.

On March 20, 1915, we agreed that Steele -should command, and I sent the following telegram to Kitchener:
I purpose appointing Major General Sam Steele to command Second Overseas Canadian Division. He is splendid organizer and disciplinarian. Do you object?
Kitchener replied as follows:
London, March 22, 1915.
General Hughes,
Minister of Militia,
Ottawa.
Reference to your telegram of twentieth March. I am sorry that in present state of warfare on the continent, it would not be possible to place General Steele in command of a division. Very experienced officers are necessary in such positions to do justice to the troops under their command.
That got me rather hot under the collar, because Steele had had a lot of these gentlemen under his command in South Africa. Some of the very best men at the front have been trained by Steele in South Africa. I am not saying that he has not his faults as an administrator, but as an organizer and trainer and commander of troops I think he would be hard to beat; and I always endeavoured to put these fellows where they would do the most good. I would not have dreamed of putting General Steele in a place of administration in comparison with some others, but I would put him in to command men. On March

29, 1915, I wired Lord Kitchener as follows:
Regret your views re Steele. Could he have done worse than at Salisbury?
I need not refer to Salisbury, where our men had to put in a winter of horror, and where the General Officer Commanding visited them only twice during the whole winter. The telegram reads:
Regret your views re Steele. Could he have done worse than at Salisbury? My opinion based on years of experience and observation in war and on manoeuvres convinces me Steele, and my brother, Colonel John Hughes, each has qualified for division as any officer in British service.-General Blank.
Then I named an officer whose name I will not repeat because he has not come to the front; he has not been heard of publicly. In other words, several names were suggested to me, and this was one of them. The telegram continues:
General Blank-seriously suggested from England. Believe I have fifty better. However, Steele could take division across and commander satisfactory to .you could be named later. How would Lowther do?
Sam Hughes.
I was willing to meet him more than half way every time. On April 1, Kitchener replied as follows:
General Hughes,
Ottawa.
Your telegram of twenty-ninth. I have no objection to General Steele coming here in charge of contingent, if it is clearly understood by General Steele that when the contingent takes the field as a division, other arrangements for its command will have to be made.
Kitchener.
That got me rather hot under the collar, as if I was going to deceive Steele! So 1 sent the following reply, which the Prime Minister, very properly in his opinion, objected to:
Ottawa, April 7, 1915.
Earl Kitchener,
War Office,,
London.
Am somewhat surprised at your 3833 cipher April 1st. Am not in habit of deceiving and Steele will certainly know exact situation. Am not dictating, merely reviewing. I know many of your major generals ; some good and capable, but many absolutely reverse, far inferior for administration in office or capability in the field to Steele or a dozen other of my officers. Have calmly and loyally remained aloof from interference with Salisbury horror and disintegration of First Canadians, but please do not ask that too much be borne. Claim no authority to manage force in field but under Army Act, Canada has absolute authority in respect to appointments. Further, offensiveness and contemptuousness of some army officers in
First Division became almost intolerable. I look to you to see that courtesy, even-handed justice and fair play are accorded to all my deserving officers.
Sam Hughes.
A good many hon. gentlemen have insisted that I should clear up matters with regard to contracting for supplies. My plan at the beginning of the war, so far as Canadian purchases are concerned, was that the director of contracts-incidentally he is a cousin of the Prime Minister-together with capable business men should have control of the purchasing for the Canadian forces, and that it should be done by public tender or universal service, and that supplies for Great Britain and the Allies should also be managed by the director of contracts. The first buying done for Canada was on the above lines and the results were splendid, except in the case of the trucks and bicycles purchased through the friend of the Minister of Finance. The second plan of purchasing that was adopted was purchasing through a sub-committee of the Privy Council. When I was in England in 1914, they prepared jointly the Orders in Council I do not know how they ever did it, for I tried it once myself. However, that plan gave place to another one, where the minister on the recommendation of the Quartermaster General and D.O.C. sent in an order in council, which was referred to a sub-committee of the Privy Council. This resulted in failure and delays, and gave place to the War Purchasing Commission under the Hon. Mr. Kemp, which I need not say was a much better system, although I think the plan I had at the very beginning of having the buying done by the director of contracts was still better. The War Purchasing Commission amounts practically to the same thing and its work has been very well done.
The fourth system of buying was by the War Purchasing Commission, using the Quartermaster General and the Director of Contracts to help them. The first subcommittee of the Privy Council ran the buying on the basis of patronage. Next the British commission was appointed, and then the War Purchasing Commission and the Munitions Board.
In regard to munitions, I may say that I do not hear the words "Shell Committee" mentioned now. To the Shell Committee and to your humble servant in inaugurating that committee, is due the financial success that Canada enjoys to-day, and to them and

Let us not forget the Shell Committee. The Imperial Munitions Board is a nice name, but I like the old Shell Committee, and I like the men that ran it.
