When was that order in council passed?

I am not sure. It was passed in my absence anyway, you may be sure of that; I have never read it yet. The point is that they said: Here you must not have so many regiments recruiting in Toronto or so many recruiting in Montreal.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think what my hon. friend -says might be misunderstood. There was not an order in council passed saying that no further battalions should be recruited, but that no further battalions should be recruited without an order in council.
The object being to prevent two or three being raised in Toronto or Montreal, for instance.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Too many being raised in one place.

Toronto has a population of 600,000. Toronto should have fifteen regiments recruiting at once; but it never had more than three. Montreal, with a population of 750,000, should have had about eighteen or twenty battalions recruiting at once. Montreal never had more than three. I do not see why my county, which has turned out nearly 5,000 men, should have one battalion being raised there with 40,000 people while Toronto should have only three with 500,000. I never could see the logic of it, and I do not now. I think that Toronto should have at least fifteen battalions going on while the counties of Ontario, Peterborough and my own county, with about
40,000	each, should be raising about one battalion each.
What was the result of that order in council? What effect did it have on recruiting?

I do not know. Recruiting has not gone on, I know that. The Minister of Public Works wanted three battalions in Winnipeg-he was not afraid of it, and I passed the order. That was when I happened to learn that this order in council to which I have referred had geen
[DOT]270

passed. I went to England and when I got back he had not yet started raising the battalion; authority had not been given; it was held up in the Treasury Board or some place and nothing had yet been done. Had I been running the show in the old way we would have had them raised in six weeks. We raised the troops for Valcartier in that time, and we would have got them in the same way. In other words, three months was lost, not in organizing the battalions, but in getting the power to organize them. I am not criticising, only there seems to be a desire to play to the gallery in connection with these munition workers. There was a drop in recruiting at all events. I have heard all sorts of stories, but I have never asked my officers. When I came back my officers made certain statements; they had been directed to go slow in recruiting, but I never asked; I do not know 'whether it is true or not.
However, seeing the falling off, seeing the need of straining every nerve we .could strain at the front, when I came back I set to work to try and get the pulse of the boys. I have always been in favour of universal service, training the boys. I did not deem conscription necessary, and it was not. I could have raised 500,000 men by voluntary enlistment. I could have raised 600,000 by voluntary enlistment without any trouble, I believe. That is only a statement; but I believe I could have done it. However, this order in council stopping the authorization of regiments was passed, and the talk came on from every hand-I presume paid for by German agents- against taking men from munition works, when we have 800,000 single men between the ages of 18 and 45 in Canada, single men not doing their duty in any way except in jobs where others could take their places.
On October 17 I wrote to the Prime Minister stating that I had come to the conclusion that we must resort to compulsory service. I take the ground to-day, I have no hesitation in telling my hon. friend from Wright (Mr. Devlin) that I would not be afraid to go into Dorchester or any other county in Quebec, to meet the intelligent electors in that county; and I am sure that they would endorse the stand I take in favour of applying the Militia Act to secure men for the army. They must know that nothing stands between them and Von Hindenburg except the British Navy. And if 50 ships of war with transports should go down, what stands between Great Britain and Von Hindenburg? If the Ger-

man navy ever overbears the British, then Von Hindenburg can march to Ottawa withaut hindrance; and then I suppose these gentlemen who have opposed our men being trained would take to the woods and leave their wives and children.
I come now to the business end of the war, and I trust not to detain you much longer. Early in the war Lord Kitchener asked for certain things. We appointed the Shell Committee, made up of General Bertram, the Carnegie Brothers, Colonel Cantley and Colonel Watts. We made shells. Canada, I see by recent statements, has received directly and indirectly upwards of $750,000,000 from shells and munitions, and the country generally, as the result of that, has been prosperous. The use of basic instead of acid steel in the manufacture of *shells was introduced, and billions of pounds -not millions-but billions of pounds of basic steel, made in Canada, have been used in place of acid steel which we would have had to import from the United States. That was done through the action of Colonel Cantley and your humble servant in the premises; and, I make no bones about it. We claim the credit, the Shell Committee and your humble servant claim the credit of introducing good times into Canada through the Shell Committee and munitions work. Bankers would not lend a dollar at that time; they were very adverse to lending money for the purpose. t The manufacture of tri-nitrotoluol was introduced into Canada, as was also that of gun-cotton, acetone from the distilleries, and other materials necessary for the production of munitions. Copper was refined in Canada for the first time. Zinc also was refined, and on the first order for zinc the British Government saved $4,000,000 owing to the difference between our price, 15 cents, and the American price, 42 cents. Hundreds of thousands of tons of lead were produced in Canada, and steps have been taken for the manufacture of nickel. Then the fish industry in Canada has been greatly stimulated and expanded. We have no conception of the value of the stimulus that has been given to the fishing industry. It is estimated that $100,000,000 a year can easily be brought into Canada through the supplying of Canadian fish to the soldiers of Canada, Great Britain and France. I am informed that the French Government-and I took this matter up direct with the French Minister of War and the Minister of Munitions-has now placed a contract for fish in Canada, and that delivery of these fish will

start very soon. I took the matter up with the British Government in connection with the supply of fish for their soldiers, and the British Government, as well as the *Canadian Government, is giving large *orders for these fish. Then we had plans laid for the development of our timber trade with the Motherland, and also for agricultural products and manufactures. Why should we not supply munitions? We are supplying men, why not munitions too?

There is a point in regard to which I should like some information, because I think it is important. My hon. friend, in one of his letters to the Prime Minister, as quoted upon page 62 of Hansard, refers to the organization in England, and he makes the statement that it is now proposed to go back to the old conditions as at the end of the first five months of the war, which my hon. friend states he is sure would produce a chaotic condition of affairs. Has the hon. gentleman any information as to what the result of that has been in England?
That is a question of hearsay, and I am not going to butt in. I have my own views and data, but I have no official authority.

My hon. friend in one of his letters makes the statement:
As you are aware, it took us four months in the midst of this great war to fight through the principles of purchasing, for the Second Division, trucks at the lowest wholesale prices.
When was it that the four months were lost?
I read a long letter -was my hon. friend not listening?-show-ing that the motor trucks should have reached England in December.
Do I understand my hon. friend to say that that is what he refers to in the letter which he addressed to the Prime Minister in regard to the delays in purchasing?
It is distinctly stated in that letter that those trucks should have been ready in December, and they were not ready in May.
That letter was not in the correspondence published.
It is not.
I would like to see it.

It is on Hansard. I am asked to back the Tory Government
and party. Yes, I will gladly back the Tory Government and the Tory party-I have done so for a good many years-but the platform must be broader than "keep Laurier and the Grits out," and action must be something different from epileptic utterances and theories re the labour wanted at home and the National Service Commission. I will back any party whose interests are the best for the welfare of our soldiers and the energetic, active, successful prosecution of the war to a victorious conclusion at any cost. There are in Canada millions of mothers, fathers, sisters and children of the 300,000 boys across the water who are wondering what Canada is doing to support these lads in every legitimate way. Canada wants another 100,000 men, maybe 300,000. They can be raised. They must he raised. Less than half a hundred battleships and their consorts of the British navy stand between Germany and sea supremacy. The right hon. the leader of the Opposition hopes for victory through famine and exhaustion; others for victory along similar lines, but should famine and exhaustion fail to materialize, and should by any mischance disaster befall Britain's navy, then there is nothing between Von Hindenburg and Ottawa, and we will have to take to the woods. Let me point out that the German papers are proclaiming that even Canada is getting near the famine stage. People are talking about compulsory thrift and that sort of bugaboo. That is published in Germany, and Germany thinks that Canada with all her resources, and with the United States at her door, is exhausted. It is the same in England with those agitations about food and meatless days. They are all published in Germany, and the German people are wondering if Britain is not on the verge of a food shortage.
Let us not live in a fool's paradise. This thing is serious, and must be treated seriously, not by theorizing but by energetic action. I have no dread of Quebec province and compulsory service. In my heart I feel that should the Militia Act be applied, our compatriots of Quebec province, following their wish for an even-handed compulsory service, will not merely be enthusiastic in volunteering, but be found to respond loyally and well. I have one aim above all others, the winning of this war; but the winning of this war will never be accomplished by theorizing; it can only

be accomplished by action, action, and still more energetic action.

Government without any exception whatsoever. The policy that we have followed from that day to this has been to prosecute this war to the utmost of the power of Canada, and our actions have been such as to attract the admiration of the world outside of this House of Commons. No one believed at the time that the war would last so long or attain the magnitude that it has since attained, but the intention of the Government from the first has been to leave nothing undone which could assist in the great cause.
The ex-Minister of Militia assembled some 30,000 or 35,000 men at Valcartier. He did it in record time. I always gave him credit for it and I give him credit foT it today. It was a great achievement on the part of the ex-minister, an achievement which will stand out in times that are to come-to assemble these men from all parts of Canada within a few weeks, organize them, equip them, give them preliminary training and send them overseas. It was not only of great assistance at the time from a military standpoint but as a matter of fact it drew attention to the Dominion of Canada throughout the world. It was a great national achievement on the part of Canada. In that organization and at that time the ex-Minister of Militia had the support of every one of his colleagues from the Prime Minister down. He said very truly that this Government, unlike the Government that was in power a few years ago, did not fight like blazes amongst themselves.
He says that he himself swore.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not understand him to say that.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The ex-Minister of Militia got generous and loyal support -and I am sure he will say it here to-day -from every one of his colleagues in connection with sending forward the first contingent. Why, the ex-Minister of Militia and myself were on such good terms that he actually-and I regard this as an evidence not only of esteem but almost of admiration-offered to make me an honorary colonel. But, Mr. Speaker, I am sorry to say that I was obliged to decline because I felt that I had not the necessary military qualifications. So that, up,on the matter of policy in regard to the Militia Department before the outbreak of the war, and in regard to the prosecution of the war after the war broke out, the ex-Minister of Militia
revised edition

and myself and all the members of the Government, as far as I know, always saw eye to eye and did everything we could to assist in winning the war. Occasionally we had differences as to methods. Temperamental differences sometimes exist. The minister might desire to do things in one way and I might think that these things should be done in another way. Particularly did those differences arise with regard to the matter of expenditures under the War Appropriation Act of 1914. Hon. gentlemen will recall that a special session of Parliament was summoned in August, 1914, and Parliament, without a dissenting voice, voted the sum of $50,000,000 in a War Appropriation Act. There was this difference between that vote and the vote for the ordinary estimates: the vote for the ordinary estimates sets out the amount that shall be expended in respect of the separate services, but this vote was a lump sum. It was proper that it should be voted that way. Parliament reposed a great deal of confidence in the Government that was to expend that $50,000,000, but nevertheless provided as a safeguard that the money, and this is the express wording of the Act, should be " expended by or under the authority of the Governor in Council." We all realize that in the hurry of getting the first contingent away we could not stand too strictly on legality. The ex-Minister of Militia went ahead, through his director of contracts and other officers of his department, and gave orders for equipment, and was never interfered with.
Might I point out that not only was he not interfered with,'but he had the direct sanction of the Prime Minister of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not only was he not interfered with, but he had the direct sanction of the Prime Minister of Canada, and he was not interfered with either by the Finance Minister or any other colleague in connection with the equipping of the first contingent. The question of the expenditure of the $50,000,000 voted by the Parliament of Canada was first raised, so far as I am concerned, about the 20th of August, 1914. It was drawn to my attention that large expenditures were being made from this $50,000,000 vote, and that in all cases competitive tenders were not called for.
Was that in 1914?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is 1914 that I am speaking of. On August 27, 1914, I wrote the following letter to the Prime
[Sir W. T. White.3
Minister, and I intend to place it on Hansard, because I want the ex-Minister of Militia to understand the position I have taken, and I think when he knows the facts he will commend the position I took:-
Ottawa, August 27, 1914.
Military and Naval Expenditures.
My dear Sir Robert,-As instructed by you I have asked my deputy to convene this afternoon a meeting of the chief officials of my department of the Militia and Marine Departments and the auditor general for the purpose of considering the question of the procedure to be adopted, in order that the public interest may be protected on the one hand and no necessary delay occur on the other, in connection with the authorization and audit of expenditure under the provisions of the Act appropriating a war credit of fifty million dollars.
Under this legislation it is clearly provided
that no expenditure shall be made save under the
general or special authority of the Governor in Council. It is apparent therefore that all contracts of every kind-for transport, munitions of war, food, clothing and other supplies __must be sanctioned by order in council. Personally I realize that in the emergency which so suddenly confronted us on the outbreak of the war prompt action had to be taken by the Militia Department, which evidently proceeded to give orders for supplies and let contracts in accordance with the custom of the past. This custom should, however, no longer be followed because of the very large amounts involved and the necessity for the Government seeing to it that large contracts should only be awarded after tenders have been called for and duly considered. Any other method of procedure can only result in improvident contracts with great waste of money to the national loss and the enrichment of individuals. What I am contending for is that the vast expenditure which we must make for military and naval defence be authorized by Council in the usual way before it is entered upon. The statute expressly provides for this and the auditor general will not he able to certify payments unless its te-ms are strictly complied with. What I have to suggest is this:	.
(1)	A complete list of contracts and expendiditure already entered into and made to be laid before Council for ratification.
(2)	All future contracts and expenditure to
be entered into and made only after Council has passed the necessary orders (gene-al or special) under the authority of the Act.	t
No delay of any consequence can possibly arise in carrying out my second suggestion. The ministers are all here and likely to be here for many months to come and we are holding Council meetings once or twice daily.
If the course I have indicated is not adopted expenditures amounting to almost one-fourth of the total annual outlay of the Dominion will be made by the officials of the two departments in question, notwithstanding that responsibility for such expenditure devolves upon all members of the Government individually and collectively.
Tours faithfully,
(Sgd.) W. T. White.
What was the motive that actuated me in sending that letter? My motive was to pro-

tect the treasury of Canada, and in my present position I conceive that to be my duty. On January 11, 1915, I addressed the following letter to the Prime Minister:-
Ottawa, January 11, 1915.
My dear Sir Robert,-During the past few days I have been outlining my budget speech, and have consequently been examining carefully into our financial situation. Frankly, on account of the huge expenditure of the war and our uncontrollable expenditure upon capital account for railways and public works, I have become exceedingly apprehensive as to our finances for the coming year. It may be necessary for us to consider the shutting down of some of our larger works, but I hope this may not occur, as it is an object to us all to continue to afford as much employment as possible. So far as our war expenditure is concerned the fact that we can obtain the money readily from the British Government should not blind us to the fact that it has to be repaid, and that in the meantime interest is running upon it. Our borrowing under this heading to the end of March will amount to sixty million dollars, upon which interest charges next year will be two and a half million dollars. If we borrow one hundred million dollars next year, the interest charge will be four million dollars, which added to the two and a half millions referred to will make a total fixed interest charge of six and a half million dollars. The additions will of course go on as long as the war lastsr I am only drawing this to your attention to show how rapidly our fixed interest charges will mount up. When we issue our Canadian war loan to repay the British Government, an even higher rate of interest will have to be paid, because our credit is not so good as that of the Imperial Government.
As you know I have been strongly desirous from the beginning that we should put forth every effort to bear our share in the burden of the war notwithstanding the expense involved. What I desire to ask now is that you will give particular attention to the matter of saving unnecessary expenditures in connection with the administration of the Militia Department during the war. No doubt a great deal of such expenditure is inevitable, but it appears to me that everything that might be considered as an extra and not really required for the equipment or substantial comfort of our troops should be omitted. Suggestions will no doubt be continually brought to our attention for the purchase of accoutrements or equipment or for other expenditure which might fairly be regarded as useful, but at the same time not indispensable.
I could mention certain equipment of that character if I so desired.
I think the Minister ought to do that.
I would respectfully ask the Finance Minister to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What I had in mind when I wrote that was a shovel.

I was mighty well aware what the hon. gentleman had in hi3 mind.
18J
. Sir THOMAS WHITE: The letter continues :-
All items of this kind should be scrutinized most carefully. I do not care to take the matter up with the Minister of Militia myself, but would suggest that you do so in view of the foregoing grave financial situation which I have drawn to your attention. I have been doing my best with the estimates, but. notwithstanding all our efforts they are bound to be exceedingly large.
Yours faithfully,
W. T. White.
I now come to the month of June of last year. The ex-Minister of Militia has criticised the appointment of an Overseas Minister of Militia as unnecessary. In that I do not agree with him. I propose to read to the House certain letters which will show clearly my views with regard to the necessity, as I regard it, of the appointment of an overseas minister. When I say necessity, I mean necessity from a financial standpoint, the necessity of safeguarding the enormous expenditures of the Dominion which have been and are being made in Great Britain:
Ottawa, June 23, 1916.
Dear Sir Robert,-
On account of the immense volume of business now being transacted by the Militia Department both in Canada and In England and the magnitude of the expenditure involved, it has occurred to me that it would be in the interests of the Government to appoint some outstanding firm of chartered accountants for the purpose of advising respecting the administrative system of the Militia Department both here and abroad and upon the matter of safeguards upon expenditure such as auditing, etc. I understand that Hon. Mr. Kemp employed the firm of Price, Waterhouse & Company with good results in establishing the excellent business system of the War Purchasing Commission. The Imperial Munitions Board has also engaged firms of auditors for the same purpose. Firms such as Price, Waterhouse & Company, Touche, Niven & Company, and Marwick, Mitchell, Peat & Company have organizations in Canada and England and would no doubt be glad to undertake such duties as I have outlined at a reasonable rate of remuneration, although the question of price for services of such importance is really of secondary character. If the idea generally commends itself to you I would suggest that you discuss it with the Paymaster General and other officers of the Militia Department. In my view nothing but good could result from such action on our part and it would I think meet with the approval of Parliament and the country.
On July 27, 1916, I directed another letter to the Prime Minister:
Ottawa, July 27, 1916.
Dear Sir Robert,-
While Sir George Perley is here I think we should consider carefully the question of our war expenditures in England. From a statement presented to me this morning by the

Dominion accountant it appears there are large outstanding liabilities and unadjusted accounts running into the millions. Personally X feel that there should be some further check upon the expenditures. No doubt the officers in charge have been doing their best, but with the responsibility of their actions devolving upon us here I feel there should be a closer connection and a more rigid supervision than has prevailed in' the past.
On August 30, 1916, 1 directed a further letter to the Prime Minister:
Dear Sir Robert,-
I am somewhat concerned over the fact that the Governor in Council exercised no control, except through officials, over our growing military expenditures in Great Britain. We must have one hundred thousand men there and we are borrowing from the British Government for military expenditures at least a million pounds a month or sixty million dollars per year. A considerable part of this sum is of course for pay, but I am satisfied that there are large expenditures for supplies and equipment. This expenditure should undoubtedly be subject to authorization by or on behalf of the Governor General in Council. As it is not practicable for the Government to deal with such expenditures here I think we should appoint a commission somewhat like the War Purchasing Commission, whose authorization would be required before any contract for supplies or equipment is entered into or any expenditure made for construction or other purposes.
That I may say was my first idea of overcoming the difficulty which we had in checking and safeguarding our war expenditures in England.
If this is not done there will be opportunity for irregularities which will undoubtedly be taken advantage of; in fact rumours of irregularities have reached me from time to time recently. My idea is that this commission should be directly responsible to the Governor in Council and should have at its head Sir George Perley, acting high commissioner. With such a commission we would have every confidence that this large expenditure was being made properly and that waste would be practically eliminated.
There is another suggestion which I have to make, namely, that a firm of chartered accountants, such as Price, Waterhouse & Company, or Marwick, Mitchell & Company, should be engaged to audit all our accounts in Great Britain. When it is considered that our expenditures there are equal to the entire expenditure made by Canada only a few years ago, the necessity for the closest possible check is apparent. Such an audit should not only' cover future transactions but past expenditures also in order that we may be assured of the regularity of the transactions which have already taken place. My view is that the auditor general should also have a representative in England as I do not believe his office here can properly audit expenditures made abroad.
As the question of expenditure so closely concerns my department I had intended making a submission to council embodying the above suggestion, but upon reflection it appeared to me that any submission should be made by yourself. I hope you will take the matter up at an early date as I am frankly anxious about the situation.

This is the letter I submit of a minister of the Crown who is desirous of safeguarding the money of the people of Canada, and throwing all proper checks around expenditures in Great Britain. It was at my suggestion that the auditor general went to England during the past year foT the purpose of looking into the situation and, if ihe found it necessary or desirable, of establishing a branch of his department in Great Britain. I submit that my course in that regard was proper from every standpoint, and I have no apology whatever to make for it. It was the sound and proper course. The auditor general went over to England, and with him and Sir George Perley we looked into the question of the expenditure of the pay office and the organization there, and I am glad to say that I came hack very much reassured as to the situation in Great Britain. The administration in Great Britain has, on the whole, been an honest one. The officials there have, as a general rule, done excellent work, having regard to the difficulties with which they had to contend.

I did not know that the Minister of Finance had all this datja here. I had intended to touch on this very aspect of the case. At the first the financial situation on the other side could not have been more rotten than it was, but I changed that in the year 1914-15. I appointed Mr. Dowie in charge of remodelling the pay office in Great Britain; I afterwards strengthened it by sending across Mr. Ross, an expert accountant of Montreal, and I could have told the hon. Minister of Finance, if he had asked me, that he would find things there better than in the city of Ottawa.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not at all clear as to that; hut I am quite clear as to this, that if we are spending sixty or eighty million dollars in Great Britain, we cannot surround that expenditure with too many safeguards.
Is the hon. Minister of Finance not aware that almost every dollar of that money spent in England is statutory expenditure?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
A great deal of it is for pay, hut a great deal of it is expenditure otherwise. Let my hon. friend make no mistake about that. The position I take in that letter is a sound course and one that will commend itself to every member ,of this House.
On October 6, 1916, I wrote another letter to the Prime Minister with regard to

the appointment of a Minister of Overseas Services. I produce the letter because I do not believe that the ex-Minister of Militia knows my true attitude with regard to that appointment. I believe he has been misled with regard to my attitude.
By whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It might be by some of his good friends on the other side. I do not know.
On October 6, 1916, I wrote this letter to the Prime Minister:
Ottawa, October 6, 1916.
Dear Sir Robert,
On August 30 I wrote you stating that I was concerned over the fact that the Governor in Council exercises no control except through officials over our growing military expenditures in Great Britain. This expenditure will soon reach an amount equal to the total annual expenditure of Canada ten years ago. After giving the matter my best consideration I am of the opinion that the time has arrived when we should have a Minister of Overseas Services who will have direct supervision and control over all our expenditures abroad and be responsible therefor in the same way as a minister here is responsible for the administration of his department. No system of administration through officials will be satisfactory, as the principle of responsibility to Parliament and the people will be lacking and grave irregularities are bound to arise for which the Government and every member thereof will be accountable. For myself I feel that the matter is vital and that I cannot assume responsibility for the acts of officials not under the immediate supervision and control of a member of the Government. In my view it is not possible for a minister here to exercise the necessary degree of supervision and control over officials carrying out such extensive and constantly increasing operations as are involved in our transactions in Great Britain. I feel that it is particularly my duty to call your attention to this subject and to express to you the opinion which I hold respecting it, as the Department of Finance is more immediately concerned and has probably, in the eyes of the public, a higher degree of responsibility for the effectual control and safeguarding of our expenditures than any other department of the Government. I commend these representations to your most earnest consideration.

Will the minister read
the answers to any of those letters?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There are no
answers. I sent them to the Prime Minister, amd no replies came to 'hand, except, possibly, acknowledgements- It was perfectly clear to all of us-not only to me as Minister of Finance, but to the Prime Minister and to the Government as a whole- that the time had arrived when, on account of our great expenditures, of the enormous forces that we bad in Great Britain and of the necessity for co-ordinating the services in Great Britain and on the Continent, a Minister of Overseas services had to be appointed. No man, I care not who he is, -could administer from Ottawa military affairs three thousand miles away, and involving as much expenditure as the whole Parliament of Canada administered ten years ago. No minister could do it successfully and as it should be done, having regard to the necessity for safeguarding the public interest. I say further that if I had been Minister of Militia, I should have insisted upon the appointment of an Overseas Minister of Militia; so that I have pretty clear views as to the necessity for taking that course.

Why not appoint
an Overseas Minister of Finance?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Because the situation does not demand it.
It is finance we are dealing with.

I beg my hon.
friend's pardon. So far as general finances are concerned, the work over there has not been very greatly increased; it is the expenditure in connection with the military situation, that has increased-
My bon, friend has animadverted to the appointment of an Overseas Minister; he has been disposed to criticise it. Well, if I read correctly the correspondence, he was willing that an Overseas Minister should be appointed. He wanted Sir Max Aitken to foe appointed.

he should have rank or title to give him authoxity-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As Minister of
Finance I consider it my peculiar duty to the citizens and taxpayers of Canada to safeguard our expenditures both here and in Great Britain to the utmost possible extent, and upon these letters that I have read to the House I may rest my ease before this Parliament or before any body of citizens in Canada.
