speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at six o'clock, I had placed before it certain letters which I had addressed to the Prime Minister, during the years 1914, 1915 and 1916, with respect to safeguarding the war expenditure of the Dominion. I may say that in the suggestions which I made to the Prime Minister I had always his entire support and the support of my colleagues. The letter of August 27,	1914,
which I read first, referred to instructions received from the Prime Minister himself; and-the suggestions which were made to the Prime Minister in the letter of August 27, 1914, were acted upon. Tnat is to say, all orders which had been given without the express authority of the Governor in Council, on account of the necessity for haste in getting forward the first contingent, were ratified by order in -council, and all subsequent orders were sanctioned by the Governor in Council before being given. Those letters embodied the principles which have actuated myself, as Minister of Finance, and actuated the Government since the outbreak of this war. I spoke in one of the letters of the matter of equipment. I stated that, having regard to the large expenditures which the Government was making and to the general financial position, it was advisable, in my opinion, that all purchases of equipment, unless clearly indispensable,'should be scrutinized closely. Now, I do not mean to suggest for one moment that the then Minister of Militia was bringing forward or was about to bring forward any proposals for the purchase of equipment which he did not regard as desirable. On the contrary, I believe this, that in the case of no belligerent in this war or in any other war has there been less waste

in the administration of the war than there has been	in connection with the
administration of this Government since the war broke out. War makes demands upon governments and governments must act quickly. The real question is whether the Government has acted, on the whole, with good judgment and in good faith.	The ex-Minister of Militia
brought forward many proposals for equipment, always in good faith. Patents were placed before him. The minister, pressed with the multitudinous duties of his office, came forward with what he thought might be of use for the purpose of protecting the lives of our soldiers at the front or giving them greater efficiency in their "work at the front. So I say, with regard to this matter of equipment which I touched upon in one of the letters, I was not suggesting for a moment that any equipment had been purchased, or was likely to be purchased, that was not, in the opinion of the minister, necessary or advisable. What I was contending for was that all things that were not clearly indispensable should be scrutinized closely. I think it is only fair to the ex-Minister of Militia that I should make that explanation. I repeat that if you take all the nations that are engaged in this war, and have regard to the scale of their operations, the mode of (purchase, the administrative acts which have been taken, their financial operations, having regard also to the proportion which must be observed between their operations and ours, in my belief there has been less waste in connection with the administration of the Militia Department	and this	Governmentof Canada than	in	connection	withthe administration	of	any	other	belligerent in the world. I say that not only with regard	to	the	present	war
but in regard to any war of the past. I say it has been possible because the Prime Minister and all the ministers of this Government, including the ex-Minister of Militia, while we have been desirous of doing our whole duty, doing everything possible to carry on this war, we have at the same time been desirous of eliminating waste so far as possible and carrying on the war in such a way that our finances would stand the strain; because this war had not been long under way before it was apparent to most of us that it would be a long war, that it would probably be determined on the principle of attrition, by the exhaustion of the combatants, and that it

was necessary to preserve, so far as possible, our credit and our resources. Apart from that, making large demands as we have been upon the tax payers of the country, borrowing heavily from the patriotism of the people, it is desirable in a large degree that the utmost economy should be exercised, having regard always to the exigencies of the wax.
I have spoken briefly with regard to the office of Overseas Minister. Some reflection has been cast upon Sit George Perley, who is not in the House. I have been desirous for a long time of paying what I regard as a much merited tribute to Sir George Perley. Sir George Perley went over to England in 1914 intending to stay as acting high com-missioijer for a few months only. But war broke out, and at great inoonveni'ence to himself, because he lives he^e, and his interests are here, he remained at his post. I wish to say that the services of Sir George Perley in the office of acting high commissioner since the war broke out have been, in my judgment, simply invaluable to Canada. I do not think that anyone in this House, outside the members of the Government, have any idea of the extent of the negotiations that have taken place between the Government of this country and the Government of the United Kingdom since the outbreak of war, of the cabling which necessarily takes place, of the financial and other transactions which have been carried out through the mediation of Sir George Perley. I was gratified in the highest degree, but not surprised-because I knew the man-to find the high standing which Sir George Perley enjoys in official, financial and other circles in London. I make bold to say that no representative, either of this Dominion or of any of the overseas Dominions, ever enjoyed a higher standing than that enjoyed by Sir 'George Penley as acting high commissioner of Canada in London.
Reference has been made also to General Turner. I was in England during the month of November, and it was during that month that the retirement of the Minister of Militia occurred. Sir George Perley consulted with me a good deal about the situation existing in Great Britain. He reached the conclusion, I think soundly, that a commander in chief was needed in Great Britain with an adjutant general, quartermaster general, inspector general, and other officers of a general staff. It was necessary, not only from the standpoint of the efficiency of the Canadian forces in the United Kingdom, but, in our judgment, and in the judgment of the Government, in order that the
work of the forces in the United Kingdom and on the Continent might be properly co-ordinated. The problem over there is to train the contingents that are sent from here, first in England, and, after they have been trained sufficiently, to send them forward to reinforce the men at the front. Reinforcements have been required on a scale undreamt of at the outbreak of the war, because the casualties have been so heavy, and if there is anything that appears clearly to me it is that, having regard to the extent of the forces in Great Britain and on the Continent at the present time, it is desirable that there should be a staff with a commander in chief, a man who knows the situation in Gres* Britain and or>
the continent, and who will assist in coordinating the British situation with the continental situation. That is precisely what the commander in chief, who has been appointed in Great Britain, will help to do. In selecting that man, regard was had to the troops at the front, and, so far as I know, no more popular appointment could possibly have been made, no better man could possibly have been appointed than General Turner. I was surprised and delighted on my visit to the front in talking with the brigadiers and colonels to find the high esteem in which every divisional commander was held by all the men at the front-General Turner, General Currie and General Lipsett. I was delighted to find the high esteem in which they were held by all the officers and men with whom I had the privilege of talking while I was there. General Turner is a man who won the Victoria Cross. He is a man of the highest standing, and is beloved by his division, and, as far as I could ascertain, by all the other commanders, brigadiers and officers in France; and, so far as I am concerned, I have no hesitation in saying that I do not believe that any better appointment could have been made. General Turner was not desirous of leaving the front. Let me make that plain. Nothing but a letter from the Prime Minister of this country asking him to accept the position, which was deemed of great importance, the position of commander in chief in Great Britain, induced him to leave the front. I think it is only fair to General Turner, as a gallant officer and a man who would much rather have remained at the front than have returned to England to assume the duties, and important duties they are, of commander in chief of the Canadian forces in Great Britain, that that explanation should be made in this House.

This afternoon the ex-Minister of Militia made a statement, which I am sorry to say reflected upon myself, with respect to Mr. T. A. Russell's connection with the purchase of motor transport. The ex-Minister of Militia stated that Mr. T. A. Russell had been recommended to him by me for the purpose of purchasing the motor transport. This statement is absolutely incorrect. I did not recommend Mr. Russell to the exMinister of Militia for the purpose of purchasing the transport for the first division. If the ex-Minister of Militia had asked me whether I would recommend Mr. T. A. Russell for the position, I would have said without any hesitation that I would, because I believe him to be a thoroughly honourable and capable man. But, as a matter of fact, I did not recommend him. As I understand it, Mr. Russell came to Ottawa to try to get an order for the Russell Motor Company, of which he was the managing director. The minister desired the transport quickly for the first contingent, and he said to Mr. Russell: I want you to buy the motor transport; you have three weeks in which to do it; and, as I understand it, Mr. Russell did the work in three weeks. Unless I am mistaken, that was the evidence given before the Public Accounts Committee.
By whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: By Mr. Russell.

Will the hon. gentleman allow me to make a correction? I had several names before me, and I remember I took the matter up in the presence of the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister. I knew that Russell had been recommended. A number of the heads of the departments had been looking for men, and I stated that Russell had been recommended. The Minister of Finance said, *' An A1 man," or words to that effect, and the Prime Minister also said he was a very good man.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I only wish to
say that the memory of the ex-Minister of Militia is not iclear. If he had 'asked whether I would recommend Mr. Russell,
I would unhesitatingly have said that I would; and if to-day I were asked if I would recommend him, I would say without hesitation that he is as good a man as we could get, a capable man, an honourable man. I .stand by that. The reflection that has been made upon me is that for some reason of interest to myself I recommended Mr. Russell, and that Mr. Russell's com-

pany made a profit upon the purchase of the transport. I repeat that I did not recommend Mr. Russell, and I did not know of Mr. Russell's appointment until after it had been. made. But after he was appointed, I decidedly said that Mr. Russell was a good man. If the matter were loft there, if there was no other evidence upon this point, the position would be that the ex-Minister of Militia says the Minister of Finance recommended Mr. Russell. Mr. Russell, according to. his statement, made a profit for the Russell Motor Company and the Minister of Finance was a friend of Mr. Russell. It was stated further that the Minister of Finance had some transactions with Mr. Russell in connection with the Cycle Motor Company. I desire to say that I never had a business transaction with Mr. Russell in my life, not to the extent of one copper.
Were you not connected with the Canada Cycle Motor Company?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The company of which I was general manager acted as transfer agents for the Cycle Motor Company. If any body wanted to transfer shares of the stock he came into the office of the National Trust Company and transferred, in the books, of the company the shares of the Cycle Motor Company. We had scores, if not hundreds, of transfer agencies and I do not know of any trust company that has not transfer agencies. Mr. Russell is connected with the 'Cycle Motor Company, as I understand. I never had a dollar's worth of interest in the Russell Motor Company. I want to say further, because I want to clear this thing up-I believe in clearing the air-that when I became Minister of Finance I proceeded to sell out every security of every kind whatsoever that I had in Canada because I did not want any one to be in the position of saying that the Minister of Finance is interested in this industry or in that industry, or in this company or in that company. That may be quixotic but I wiant to make that statement; it is true. Just to clear this up a little more-

I wish we had all sold
about that time.
We should have all sold out just about the time this Government came in.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend will look at the quotations on the stock exchanges to-day, and I have no doubt he is fully posted on them-

That is owing to the
war.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If he will look at the quotations, I think he will find a degree of prosperity that this country has never had before.

That is what they call
war bride stocks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
, Now, one word on another matter referred to by the ex-Minister of Militia, because I do not think he wants to be unfair to me. After the transports had been bought for the first contingent, it was brought to the attention of my hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) that a commission had been paid in connection with the purchase of transport to a firm in Ottawa on a sale by the Ottawa Car Company of certain transport. It was alleged that Mr. Russell had bought this transport and the implication was that he had been a party to the paying of a commission. We did not know the circumstances under which that commission was paid. Mr. Russell having concluded his work in purchasing the transports for the first contingent, I had given to him, as I had given to scores of business men in Canada, a letter of introduction to Sir George Perley because he was going over to England to eee if he could sell some transports to the British Government. I heard that Mr. Russell had been appointed a purchasing agent for the British Government. I had every confidence in Mr. Russell but nevertheless, as soon as I heard the suggestion that a commission had been paid which might have been improperly paid in connection with the purchase of transports from the Ottawa Gar Company, I sent this cable to Sir George Perley:
Ascertain and cable whether T. A. Russell whom X introduced to you has been appointed as purchasing agent for British Government as reported here. Sorry to state there has been grave criticism of his buying for-Militia Department here. If he is purchasing for War Office ask him to see you and show him this cable. Important.
I got a cablegram back frtrn Sir George Perley, in which he said that:-
Have seen Russell who says he has not been appointed purchasing agent for British Government except that he arranged through another firm to buy in United States some goods for War Office about which he wrote fully to Doctor Reid but which for war reasons ought not he generally known. I am writing you some particulars by to-day's mail. Russell has also been asked by War Office report on some large machines when he returns home early in December.
The letter to Doctor Reid refers only to matters of customs. When Mt. Russell came back from England I asked 'him to come to Ottawa and we held a Treasury Board meeting, at which the Solicitor General was present. We asked him for an explanation of the commission of the sale by the Ottawa Car Company. He gave a full, direct and entirely satisfactory explanation and I wrote to Sir George Perley as follows:-
Ottawa, January 5, 1915.
Personal.
My dear Sir George,-At my request Mr. T. A. Russell, to whom I gave a letter of introduction to you some time ago, appeared to-day before the Treasury Board with reference to purchase for the Militia Department of transport necessary for the first contingent. In view of my cable to you I think it only proper to say that Mr. Russell's explanations were not only entirely satisfactory to the members of the Committee but such as to entitle him to the thanks of the Government for the untiring intelligence and zeal displayed by him In arranging for the purchase within a period of twenty days of the entire transportation equipment of the first contingent. There has been much ill-founded criticism by interested parties but we are all satisfied that Mr. Russell's conduct throughout has been wholly exemplary. He had a most difficult task to perform and carried It out, in my judgment at least, with very great ability. As Mr. Griffith saw the cable which I sent you I shall be glad if you will acquaint him with the contents of this letter.
With kind regards.
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd.) W. T. White.
Hon. Sir George Perley,
London.
That looks as if I were interested in Mr. Russell making commissions for the Russell Motor Company. If the ex-Minister of Militia, in view of the correspondence and of the statement I have made, believes it, all I have to say is that I am sorry for him.
Before six o'clock I stated that I understood the ex-minister had been willing that an overseas minister should be appointed, provided that the minister was Sir Max Aitken. I accepted the statement that the ex-minister made, that that was not his intention, but the statement made in his letter of October 26, 1916, which possibly has been before the House, is this:-
But I will be more than proud to support the proposition, with all my heart and all my power, if you fill in the name of Sir Max Aitken. It is a question of the man and not the office.
Read the next letter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Which one?

The hon. gentleman must know that if there is one letter there

must be others. Read the next letter. Be fair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Very well; hut, however, I accept the explanation of my hon. friend and I am quite willing to take his statement that he was opposed to the appointment of an overseas minister of militia. I think I have cleared up nearly all the matters touched upon by the exMinister of Militia except the question of delay in the purchase of transports. My own recollection in regard to it, although, as a matter of fact, I had very little to do with it, is that there was some delay as to whether Kelly-Springfield or some other truck was the better truck. But my recollection is that the'ex-Minister of Militia appointed a committee for the purpose of determining that, and whatever delays took place were delays inseparable from making a decision on the very important subject of motor transportation. That is all I desire to say cpon that.
There are one or two observations I desire to make upon the general debate. I do not propose to generalize, but I am sorry, and I think many members of this House are sorry, as well as many people of this country, that in some respects this debate has degenerated into a petty political controversy. I have no desire- to generalize, I say, because it would be unfair. Some notable speeches, some serious speeches, some earnest speeches have been made, but it seems to me that there has been a lot of idle talk about patronage and appointments and Nationalists. Here we are in the midst of the greatest war in the world, a war in which we are engaged as belligerents; the flower of our youth at the front; others of our sons in the United Kingdom ready to go to the front, and thousands in Canada ready to cross the seas. We are at the very crucial period of the war-the third and probably the decisive year, the year in which the greatest battles in the history of the world will be fought, the year in which the greatest strain will be imposed upon the belligerents, the year of defeat or of victory, and yet in this House some of us are talking about patronage, appointments, and Nationalists, and assailing the Government for trying to make capital out of the war.
For making political capital out of the war, not for trying to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There has been a good deal of talk about lack of leadership, 
and slackness in carrying on the war, but I say, and history will confirm what I say, that there is absolutely no *room for national self-depreciation. Canada, and the Government of Canada, have played a great and noble part in this great war. Take your minds back two-and-a-half years ago, when the ex-Minister of Militia was assembling his troops at Valcartier. I gave him credit for that this afternoon,_ and I give him credit now. It was a great achievement. Let any man in this House or in this country ask himself what he would have thought at that time if it had been suggested to him that this country, peace-loving Canada, unprepared for war, composed of mixed races, diverse nationalities, a heterogeneous population of eight million, scattered over a territory as large as Europe, as large as the United States of America, would in two-and-a-half years, recruit, organize, equip, and train an army of 425,000 men; The only people who 'belittle that achievement are partisans. The organization of this great army has commanded the admiration of the world. Go to New York; what do they think about it there? Go to London; what do they think about it there? They never hear of it without greeting it with cheers. What room is there for national self-depreciation? What room is there for criticism of this Government in connection with the raising of an army of 425,000 men under the conditions I have mentioned? It is wonderful. There is not a man here, I do not care what his imagination, that could have forecasted it or would have believed it possible.
What about finance? Canada, a borrowT-ing country before the war, a country that had never made a single loan of more than six million pounds, and borrowing in London a million dollars a day, or three hundred million a year, for the Dominion Government, Provincial Governments, railways and other companies, borrowing in Great Britain principally, and also in the United States, Canada was suddenly confronted with the war, and the dislocation of business that it caused. From the very beginning, so far as it has been possible to me, and so far as it has been possible to this Government, we have aimed to maintain financial and industrial and commercial stability. We have aimed to maintain confidence, and confidence lies at the very root of prosperity, and the prosperity of this country to-day is the best evidence of the confidence

we have succeeded in maintaining in this country. Six months dislocation of business at the outbreak of the war. And yet what have we succeeded in doing? The hon. member for Piet-on, (Mr. Macdonald) is worrying as to who is to get the credit. We -never stopped, to con-siaer who was to get the credit. This is not a boys' school. Sufficient fo.r us if the thing is done. The main thing -is to get the big things done and that is what the Prime Minister has been doing, and what his ministers have been doing. We have not worried about who i-s to get the credit.
I have spoken of the effect on the world of the raising of an army of 425,000 men in Canada. Let me speak now of the effect on the world of what Canada has done in a financial way. Canada was- a borrowing country before the war. A loan had never been made in Canada, except perhaps a little currency loan thirty or forty years ago. What have we done -since the outbreak of the war, and by " we " I mean the people of Canada. I always give the credit to the people of Canada. The Government are the instruments; we take the initiative; choose the time for the loan; see that market conditions are favourable, and the -people do the rest. I do not care whether you call it leadership o-r no-t. All I want is results, and we get the results. What have the results been? In 1915 we asked the people of Canada for $50,000,000, and they gave u-s $100,000,000. Last November we asked the people of Canada for $100,000,000, and they offered us $200,000,000. Canada has financed her war expenditure on this side of the Atlantic -since the outbreak of the war and that in itself -is a notable achievement, but that is on-ly the beginning of what -she has done. What else has -she done in a financial way? The Dominion of Can-ad-a has advanced $150,000,000 to the Imperial Treasury to purchase munitions on this side of the Atlantic, and in addition to that, we have arranged for a credit of $100,000,000 from the chartered banks of Canada, making a total of $250,000,000, which we have placed to the credit of the Imperial Government for the purpose of purchasing munitions in this Dominion. Is not that an achievement? Consider the prosperity of this country to-day. There are high prices, of course, for agricultural and other products. But what of the munitions output, so large a portion of our exports? The prosperity of the country is related to agriculture and our other productions and to the production of munitions.
Now, I am going to give the ex-Minister of Militia a good deal of credit in connection with the establishment of the Shell Committee. He and I sometimes differ, but we always differ in an open way. The ex-minister deserves credit for originating the idea. An idea may be developed, but the -man who originates it deserves a great part of the credit. The ex-Minister of Militia believed in the industries of this country and he started the Shell Committee, and 1 give him credit fo.r starting it; but at the same time do no-t let us altogether lose sight of the fact that the financing of it has had something to do with the result. An exchange situation exists to-day, by reason of the fact that Great Britain is importing so much from thi-s continent, by reason of the fact' that the exchanges have partially broken down, under which Great Britain can purchase munitions on this side of the Atlantic only if she can raise money with which to pay for them on this side of the Atlantic. That statement is absolutely true; in fact, it falls short of a full statement, because she not only has to borrow, on this side of the Atlantic, all the money required to pay for her enormous purchases on this side of the Atiantic, but she actually has to borrow money on this side of the Atlantic to support the exchange, so that it is a fact that Great Britain can not purchase in Canada unless Great Britain is financed in Canada. Finance lies at the basis of Great Britain's purchases in Canada just as finance lies at the basis of Great Britain's purchases in the United States. What does that mean? That means that the $250,000,000 that we provided for the Imperial Government has meant that she was able to give the orders for munitions in Canada during the past twelve or fifteen months. No -leadership! I do not care whether you call it leadership or not. Whait would leadership be under -those circumstances? Would it do more than provide the $250,000,000 or $300,000,000? If there is anything more that leadership would do, I would like my Ihon. friend the member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) or any one else to tell me. - No leadership! No one would have dreamed of such a (thing happening. Ask any financial -man in Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, or any other place you like, if -two or three years ago he would have believed the Dominion of Canada would pay her own war expenditures, amounting as it does to the tremendous sum of $1,000,000 a day, and would, in addition to that, (h-ave been able to provide $250,000,000 for the Imperial Government for purchasing

in Canada. He would have laughed at you. Is there any room for national seM-depre-oiation? Has there been no leadership? The prosperity of this country .is to-day abounding. There is no belligerent country in anything like the condition in which we are, financially, commercially or industrially. Not a man who will work is out of work in this country to-day; wages are 'higher than they have ever been, and yet it is said that there is no leadership. Our Ihon. friends opposite accused us of lack of leadership. I cannot help but think of the story that is told of Abraham Lincoln and General Grant. My right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), who is fond of history, the other night accused the Prime Minister of indecision.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Amongst other things.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) is a great admirer of Abraham Lincoln. Let us bear in mind what has been accomplished. We have recruited 425,000 men; we have financed ourselves and Great Britain, and let us also remember the prosperity that exists in this country to-day. And yet my right hon. friend says that the Prime Minister is guilty of indecision. Abraham Lincoln appointed General Grant as Commander in Chief of the forces of the United States. Grant had some enemies who sent word to Lincoln: "He drinks!" Lincoln replied: "What brand of whisky does he use? I want it for my other generals." If that brand of leadership has produced that magnificent result, why, lack of leadership would not be a bad thing for the Prime Ministers of Canada from this time forth, to say nothing of those in the past, such as my right hon. friend. My right hon. friend has an imagination. Let me appeal to it. Years ago we used to talk of the total trade of Canada as being $500,000,000. The year before the war the total trade of Canada, exports and imports, amounted to $1,000,000,000, and we congratulated ourselves upon the fact. It was wonderful that the total trade of Canada should be one-fifth of the total trade of Great Britain. Canada was coming on. For the first six months of the year just past the total trade of Canada exceeded $1,000,000,000, which was the high-water mark for the year preceding the war, and this year we ?hall have a total trade of over $2,000,000,000. And yet my hon. friends say there is no leadership. Of course, being modest men, we give the credit to the public. If my right hon. friend had found a condition

like it he would take the credit for the party. We say that under our administration the favour of Providence, and the energy and intelligence and patriotism of the Canadian people, all these things have been accomplished.
In 1912, 1913 and 1914 the balance of trade was against us, $300,000,000,	$200,000,000
and $140,000,000, and there has been a balance of trade against us for many years past. This year, however, there will be a balance of trade of probably three ot four hundred million dollars in our favour. Yet, my hon. friends say there is no leadership. Well, if no leadership gives such magnificent results as that there is a good deal to be said for it. Now, I am not particular whether we get the credit or not. After all, this is not a boys' school.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It looks like it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It does sometimes, when I look at the other side of the House, not only a boys' school, but when I hear some of the followers of my right hon. friend speak I think it is an infants' class. We are content with the results.
What is required of Canada? We are in the third and crucial year of this war. Talk all the election talk, talk all the partisan talk you like in the House of Commons, but we are in a year of the greatest events in the history of this war, and talk of that kind will make but little impression and will not last long. I was in England during November-
So the ex-minister said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-and I want to tell hon. gentlemen that the seriousness of this situation dawns upon one when he visits England and France. We are 4,000 miles from the western battle-front, but when you are in England, France or Belgium you realize what war means. You see the fleet, as I saw it-and in my opinion the fleet of Great Britain, which is the greatest human agency to-day between the Hohenzollerns and the domination of the world, was never actually or relatively as strong as it is to-day. When you see that fleet; when you see the great body of clean-cut, strong men who, day in and day out, in summer and in winter, in heat and in cold, maintain that monotonous and weary vigil which means the safety of our commerce and the preservation of our civilization, you realize that the Empire is at war. And when you go to the front and see the men there-the officers living in dug-outs comprising two little rooms, cold

and damp; when you see the men going into the trenches and coming out encased in mud; when you observe the uncomplaining, cheerful demeanour of these men who daily walk with death, you realize what this war means, because these are our boys. There is little patience at the front with talk of patronage, appointments or Nationalism, and there will be less patience with it as the war goes on. No thinking man can visit the fleet and visit the front without coming away profoundly impressed with the terrible seriousness of this war, and that impression will grow more and more upon the people of Canada, of the Emprie and of the world as the war proceeds during the present, as I believe, crucial year. That is the spirit in which we should give consideration to the important matters of public business before us, and that, I believe, is the spirit in which the great majority of the members of this House are approaching them-a spirit which exemplifies a realization of the seriousness of the war and which is manifested in its deepest sense by men who have sons there and by men who have lost their sons.
It devolves upon every member of this House and every citizen of Canada to do his part. The Prime Minister cannot be on every platform of Canada, week in and week out. He has spoken scores of times since this war broke out; so have I, and so have other members of the Government. We have been necessarily oppressed with business since the war broke out. Transactions with the Imperial Government, matters relating to the troops in England and at the front, the organization of our troops in Canada, matters arising out of the dislocation of business which is inevitable when a war is proceeding, international questions, matters of the utmost moment and importance-these are the burdens which from day to day, from week to week, morning, noon and night, Saturday and Sunday, have been borne by the Prime Minister and his colleagues. We are not complaining; it is our duty, and we do it. But it is open to any member of this House to do his best to impress the public mind with the necessity for men and munitions and the necessity of saving for the purpose of assisting the financing of the war. I believe that most of the members have done this, and I am quite sure that they will continue to do so. What is required at the present time, not only in Canada and the United Kingdom, but
throughout the entire world, is organization and the creation of a certain attitude of mind on the part of the public with relation to this war. The great majority of the people are seized with the importance of the war, but many are not, to the same degree. There must be man organization; there must be organization of vital industries; production must be stimulated and increased as much as possible. There should be no personal or public extravagance, and there should be national saving, because in the last analysis it will be money and resources as well as. men that will win this war. There must be selfdenial and there must be self-sacrifice. The men at the front are undergoing sacrifices cheerfully and uncomplainingly; it is not too much to ask every person to exercise self-denial and self-sacrifice in
9 p.m. order that he, too, may contribute to the utmost of his power to the winning of the war.
A great number of important questions are mooted from time to time-important, but secondary and subsidiary questions. The real question before the Empire to-day is the winning of the war, and nothing else. How do governments, oppositions, individuals, measure up against the great question of winning the war? That is the question to which the governments of all the communities in the Empire must direct themselves. The British nation was slow in getting organized for the war, because it was so entirely unprepared at the outbreak of hostilities. In Great Britain these questions were met as they arose, and to-day I believe that the nation is very highly organized. Millions of men have been sent to the front; no one ever expected that more than 200,000 or 300,000 men would be sent from England to Europe. The loans that have been raised by the British Government would have staggered the imagination of men before the war broke out.
The Government since the outbreak of this war has addressed itself to the utmost of its ability and power to the great questions that have been presented for its consideration. The successes which we have met with-with the co-operation and support, of course, of the Canadian people, because the Government can do nothing without that-are exemplified in the statements which I have made to the House with regard to the recruiting of our forces and our finances and trade. I repeat that there is absolutely no room for national

self-depreciation, but I am the first to say that we can do better. We can all do better. We have gone so far; we can go much farther. The Government will continue to put forth its best efforts as in the past, and I am perfectly confident that, putting forth ,our best efforts, with the rest of the overseas dominions putting forth their best efforts, with the mighty effprt which Great Britain is putting forth, with the heroism and the sacrifices of France and the efforts which she will put forward in the future, this war is going to be won this year.

Mr. Speaker, there are some remarks which my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) has made with which I am sure we will all agree. The one that strikes me as being the most important is that all the people of Canada should be united in a determination to do the utmost that is possible in assisting in bringing this war to <a successful conclusion. My hon. friend has very frankly stated that we could all do much better than we have done. With regard to the Government, Sir, I think we will all be disposed to agree with him. We will all agree that the Government, if it applied its mind, if it applied the united efforts of its members, could do a great deal better than it has done in the past, and, may I add, Sir, the hope that after the expression which my hon. friend has used, that the Government can do better than it has done, it will make a sincere effort to do better and to perform a 'service which will entitle it even in some -measure to the gratitude and confidence of the people of this country, because, Sir, let me assure my hon. friend, as I believe, that no one upon this side of the House is desirous of seeing this Government lost the confidence of the people of this country merely in order that my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and hon. gentlemen upon this side of the House, may assume the seals of office. We have no especial personal desire for. that. Speaking for myself, 1 would assure you, and I do assure you most earnestly, that I never was so happy since the day I first entered political life as I have been in opposition; and my pleasure has been increased by the fact, Sir, that I have been engaged in the worthy cause of attacking a Government which, I believe, is not deserving of the confidence of the people of this country. That, Sir, is a worthy object for any body of men. To dp one's duty as a member of His Majesty's
fPir W. T. White.]
loyal Opposition is to perform one of the noblest services which a public man can render to his country. Therefore, dn all sincerity, I express the hope that from this moment this Government will turn back upon its tracks, will reverse the course which it has pursued in the past, and will endeavour well and faithfully to serve the people of this country. It may be too late for them to regain the confidence of the people; it may be, but still it is not too late for them to try.
Now, Sir, my hon. friend says that in this House and in this country there is an attempt to make party capital. I interjected a remark to that effect when my hon. friend was speaking. If I were asked for proof, I should give it in the fact that ever since this war broke out this Government and its supporters throughout the Dominion have endeavoured, so far as they could, to make their conduct of the war the means of increasing their party influence and a stepping stone to their return to power. The Minister of Finance says that, being now in the third year of the war, the most strenuous year in the history of the war, our attention should be entirely directed to the winning of the war, and that we should not stop to give consideration to such questions as patronage, and partyism, and nationalism and questions of that kind. What does that mean, Sir? . It means that the Government should not be criticised for using patronage in the making of war contracts; it means that they should not be criticised for the effort to strengthen their party with the people of this country by passing money and patronage into the hands of their supporters or those whom they hope will become their supporters. And this, Sir, when there are in that Government, members of the Nationalist party. We have the evidence before us that in 1910 the Nationalist party of Quebec first took the unpatriotic ground, laid it down as a matter of policy for the people of Canada which they at all events were determined to support in Quebec; that Canada should take no part in the wars of the Empire, that neither the money, nor the men, nor the ships of Canada should be sent beyond the confines of this Dominion; and they appealed to the prejudices of the people who had confidence in them to stand by thedr policy as against any participation in the wars of the Empire. From that day to this we have seen the Nationalist party in Quebec adhering to that position, and, Sir, only two or three days ago, we had the spectacle of the Postmaster General (Mr. Blondin) going

down into a constituency in the province of Quebec where a by-election was being held, and declaring to the people there that they need have no fear of conscription, because, if it came into force their young men could easily cross the boundary into the United States and so escape from the effects of the war. And yet we find that gentleman, so far as we can judge from the statements of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, still enjoying the confidence of his colleagues. So it comes with ill grace from the Minieter of Finance to taunt us with speaking of Nationalism and condemning Nationalism on the floor of this Parliament.
Then, Sir, what further have we so far as patronage is concerned? We have the statement made in this House, we have the statement made in this country, made without contradiction, because it is impossible to contradict it, that even in the case of soldiers, even in the case of our boys who have gone to the front prepared to make the supreme sacrifice for their country, when they have returned wounded and have asked for positions which they could properly fill, they have been referred by the committee having the matter in charge to the patronage committee representing the Government of this country, speaking for the Conservative party in this country, and they have been obliged to get the recommendation of this patronage committee before they could be appointed to fill any position! S'ir, only a few days ago, in the city of St. John, there was a meeting of the recruiting committee, and I am now going to quote from what took place at that meeting as supporting the statement which I make, and not merely the statement, but supporting the charge, a charge which this Government ought to be ashamed to lie under, supporting the charge that even in the case of the returned soldier the question of whether a man has belonged to a Liberal or to a Conservative family is to determine whether he is to get employment, is to determine whether or not his country is to recognize the sacrifice which he has made for the flag. Well, Sir, this meeting in St. John was presided over by a gentleman whom the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) knows well, presided over by one of the most prominent *Conservatives in the province of New Brunswick, a gentleman who not long ago was appointed by the Conservative Government in the province of New Brunswick as one of the directors of a company which is constructing that important line of railway known as the St. John Valley railway; I refer to Mr. Richard O'Leary, of the county of Kent, in the province of New Brunswick. At that recruiting meeting in the city of St. John, on the 3rd of January last, as reported in the St. John Telegraph of 4th January, Mr. O'Leary said:-
In spite of the resolution, it still is necessary for even a returned soldier to secure the recommendation of the patronage committee before he can secure a Government appointment.
That was the statement made by a gentleman who has been closely identified with recruting in the province of New Brunswick, who was chairman of the recruiting meeting for that province; a gentleman of the very highest standing, who has given of his wealth and time to every patriotic cause in New Brunswick since the war began; and that statement is simply confirmatory of what hon. gentlemen have stated on the floor of this House as to what is going on in this country. And yet my hon. friend the Minister of Finance says: Oh, because the war is on, and because our united effort should be directed towards the winning of the war, you must not speak of patronage; you must let us exercise it to the fullest extent in respect to our supporters throughout the country, and you must not make any complaint or criticism. Why, not long ago, the newspapers reported my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) as having gone to the city of St. John and given a banquet to his patronage committee who are making these recommendations for the filling of positions of this character and of other positions which come under the control of the Government.
We have had an extraordinary exhibition this afternoon and evening. Although Parliament has been sitting now for some days, we have had no explanation by the ministry as to the reasons why the Minister of Militia was dismissed from office. The ex-Minister of Militia is not in the position of one who resigned; he was dismissed from office. The letter of the Prime Minister to him shows clearly that this is the position in which he stands. Ordinarily, in such circumstances, ministerial explanations are made. Ordinarily, the Prime Minister takes Parliament and the country into his confidence, and gives the reasons for ministerial changes; but the Prime Minister has not done this House or the people of this country the courtesy of giving the explanations which a Prime Minister always thinks well to give in such circumstances. It has remained until this

afternoon and evening for us to hear something of the reasons for the change which has taken place. The statements made by the ex-Minister of Militia and the Minister of Finance lead us to believe that very many more statements might have been made and very much more information might have been given to the people of this country as to the reasons why the change took place. My hon. friend, the ex-Minister of Militia, is clearly holding himself in leash. It would break his heart to separate from his dear Conservative friends, he says.
Hear, hear.

He says it would almost give him as much anxiety and as much sorrow to do that as if we were to lose the war. Loving his Conservative friends as he does, he holds himself in apparent restraint in order that he may still have a bridge across which he may walk backwards and again get into the confidence of his party. Perhaps between the time when he informed the public through the newspapers that he was going to make a full statement, and to-day, he has heard rumours which have come across the Atlantic that it will not be long before there is a change in the high commissionership, and that some other gentleman, possibly one who stands high in the Government of this country, may take the place of the gentleman who now occupies that position. It is not impossible that my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Militia may think that when the changes that may come about in the whirligig of time, possibly within a few weeks, take place there may be an opportunity for him to go back. Perhaps he feels that it is due to himself that he should not say too much or say anything that would prevent him from returning to the fold. But he tells the House that, for the first ten months of his administration of the Militia Department, he was continually hampered in his work; that he was treated as a responsible minister ought not to be treated, and that in the Cabinet he had two enemies. He uses polite language, the language of Parliament, but he tells us there were two enemies who constantly intrigued against him and prevented him from carrying on the great work which he felt he ought to do in his department in the interests of Canada and of the Empire.
How does my hon. friend the Minister of Finance answer that? Does he give us
fMr. Pugsley. ]
an explanation? He says there was something relating to trucks in regard to which the ex-Minister of Militia made some recommendation. He was getting information as to the Kelly truck or some other truck, and that it took some time to decide. That is what my hon. friend the Minister of Finance says. But that is not the charge made by the gentleman who for five years was the trusted colleague of the Prime Minister, the gentleman who for five years was entrusted by this Government with the duty of managing the military affairs of this country. I will read what he says in his letter to the Prime Minister dated May 13, 1915. So far from agreeing with my hon. friend the Minister of Finance in what he states regarding the little matter of trucks and the delay that was caused, this is what the ex-Minister of Militia says:
Dear Sir Robert:	Since my return from
England last November, I have repeatedly notified you that owing to the interference and plans of the "so-called" sub-committee and to the repeated hold-ups and needless obstructions of some of my colleagues in the affairs of this department-
Will the Minister of Finance take notice? If the Minister of Public Works were here I would ask him to take notice also.
-the Contract branch has been very much hampered and practically blockaded; delays have been very prolonged; the cost has been greatly enhanced and the goods supplied have been, in many cases, inferior. Indeed, the most ardent agents of the German government could scarcely have been more successful in holding up the proper equipment of our forces, had they been in control.
Mr. Speaker, did you ever read a more serious charge than that made by a retiring minister against his colleagues with a war on? When a few weeks' delay might mean the cost of thousands of lives, and might materially affect the fortunes of war; when there was necessity for the utmost haste, the ex-minister says that he was not only not given a free hand, but was not even allowed to do that which other ministers claimed the right to do, to carry on the detail work of his department. But, by means of this .sub-committee, which *was appointed apparently behind his back, appointed for the purpose of taking control really of his department and, may I not also say, Sir, appointed for the purpose of enabling those gentlemen who were hostile to the then Minister of Militia to succeed in eventually driving him out of office-by means of this sub-committee- I say, contracts were held up, our soldiers were delayed and the most serious results

therefore necessarily would follow. Has the Minister of Finance, in whose presence that letter was read, iany answer to make to that charge? If that charge is true, Sir, it ought to bring upon this 'Government the strongest possible condemnation of the the people. Every man, every woman, every boy, whether at the front or in Canada, whether still fighting the battles of the Empire, or whether he is one who has returned -after doing his duty and being wounded is no longer able to be at the front, must feel that if that charge is true the Government must stand condemned at the bar of public opinion. Yet, Sir, notwithstanding that most serious charge, made in this House of Parliament, made before the people of this country, a charge which, to-morrow morning wil-l go- broadcast in the press of this country from the Atlantic to the Pacific, the Minister of Finance, has either not found it possible, or has not deemed it desirable, to attempt to give to this Parliament -and the people any answer. Then, the ex-Minister of Militia gives an example. He says:
As one of many specific examples, take the trucks for the second division. They should have been ready last December.
Think of that, Mr. Speaker, this sub-committee -apparently h-as had the matter o-f the trucks in charge since the previous December. Although the truok-s ought to have been ready in December they are not ready even -as -late as the 13th of May.
They should have been ready last December, and they are not ready yet. -Some ot my colleagues constituted themselves champions of this or that truck, and brought about delays whereby untried trucks would he purchased; high prices would he paid in commissions to agents, and the Government, and the country, would be treated practically as a retailer. My policy, as you may remember, in this and in all other matters, was to force dealers to give the Government wholesale, or manufacturers' rates.	-	'
If thdre is -any answer to be made to that letter, any answer to be- made to these two paragraphs, if any reply can he made, to the most .serious charge which is- contained dm these two- paragraphs, is it not due to this House, to the people and to the Government themselves that they should -make -an .answer to that charge to Which the Minister of Finance should have made a reply while -he was addressing the House this evening? Not one word of a -reply -has been m-ade. If the ex-Minister of Militia is the kind of gentleman whom this -Government -must have thought him to be when they placed him in charge of this -most important department, if he is
the man they have thought him to be for five long years in the' midst of the greatest war in history, and in the midst of the first great war in which our country has been engaged, if they have allowed him to control that important department having an expenditure of millions upon millions of the people's -money -and if he is the high minded gentleman whom we must believe him to be, and whom they believed him to be, surely there is -a duty cast upon the Government to endeavour to answer the most serious charge contained in these two paragraphs. Then, he says:
At the present time there are upwards of one hundred requisitions that have long been in.
These aTe requisitions for the soldiers; these are war -supplies which are necessary to- be issued to the soldiers before they can go to the front.
The Quartermaster General has over and over again, until his heart has grown sick, brought them before me; they have been promptly passed on to the director of contracts, and the great majority of them when passed on to the Privy Council have been held up in council, or by the Treasury Board, laid aside or sent hack 

but always delayed; while the director of contracts and his officers have unceasingly been interfered with, delayed, and given endless and unnecessary work by the sub-committee.
Where is the answer to that? Has the Prime Minister any answer? No, apparently not. The Minister of Finance has not attempted to give any answer and we have a right to assume that it is because no answer can be given, because these hon. gentlemen must know it is true. Is it not too horrible to conceive of, to think that when our boys needed these supplies, no proper effort was made -to furnish them? The ex-minister states that more -than one hundred requisitions have long been made, that the Quartermaster General, whose duty it is to furnish the -supplies, has over and over again, until his heart had grown sick, brought them before him, that they have been promptly passed on to the director of contracts by the minister, that they have been forwarded to the Treasury Board and they have -been held up, laid aside, or sent back and always delayed. Is it not a sad thing to think that when these articles were required- were absolutely required-in order to enable Canada to take her part in the carrying on of this war, they, simply through apathy, the indifference of the ministers, through some o-f them, as the ex-Minister of Militia says, wanting an article purchased from one manufacturer and others wanting an article purchased from another



manufacturer, and not being able to come to a conclusion for months and months, have been held back and the director of contracts has not been able to get his wants supplied? Could you think of a more serious charge to make, one which reflects more strongly upon the indifference and inefficiency of the Administration, than the *charge made'by the ex-Mini.ster of Militia contained in the paragraphs which I have just read? Then, he says:
I saw, by an article in the Free Press, that it is current talk everywhere among the soldiers and officers that they are short of nearly every class of equipment and supplies. In fact, three times recently I have been severely reproached about shortages in supplies and equipment by outsiders who had learned of these shortages from soldiers and officers of the force.
Here is another very serious charge regarding the medical department:
Further, to my surprise, I was spoken to in Montreal this week, and informed that our medical units going over were only half equipped, while many of our combatant units are not properly outfitted. In addition to the serious aspect of the case, and from the viewpoint of the efficiency of our soldiers, there is the disheartening side. It is not only unfair to the gallant boys who are giving and will-iiigly risking their lives for the cause, and making domestic sacrifices, but it is absolutely unjust to me and my officers.
There is the wail thait goes up from the heart, (apparently, of (the ex-Minister of Militia demanding that his boys, as he is proud to call the Canadian soldiers*, should *be promptly and adequately supplied with those things which they required to enable them .to perform their duty to their country. He tells the Prime Minister that these requisitions are tied up by the sub-committee of Council or tied up in Council until *it has made him heartsick and until it has made the Quartermaster General heartsick as well. Yet there is no reply. There is no attempt on the part of the Prime Minister to explain or excuse, and no attempt on the part of the Minister of Finance to deny or excuse. The ex-Minister of Militia goes on:
Therefore, as Minister of Militia, I must respectfully enter my protest, as I have frequently before entered it, at the interference and delays caused in all these things. It tends not only to the injury and inefficiency of our soldiers, thus jeopardizing the success of the British arms, but it must politically reflect seriously upon the Government.
I need not read any more from this letter, as it has been read by my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Militia, and will appear in Hansard. I think I have read sufficient to
fMr. Pugsley.]
show that it discloses a most serious state of affairs during the time the ex-minister was a member of the Government. It was" written as long ago as May 13, 1915, and yet for a year and a half after that time, a year and a half after the ex-Minister of Militia had made this heart-rending appeal to the Prime Minister to assist him in seeing that necessities were supplied to our soldiers promptly, the minister continued as a member of the Government, and still had the confidence of the Prime Minister, and still, apparently, enjoyed the confidence of the majority of his colleagues. We must believe that the statements he makes here he would not make except from positive knowledge. We must believe those statements are absolutely correct, and as I said before, if they are correct, I want to know what more damning accusation could be brought against a government? In the face of these charges, does it lie in the mouth of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance to tell us we ought not to criticise the Government, but ought simply to join with them and do our part in winning this war; that we ought not to criticise, or find fault, or point out defects in the Administration. Sir, I would want nothing more than this letter of the ex-minister to justify my conscience in bringing these matters to the attention of Parliament. If any member of Parliament under these circumstances declined to bring a matter of this kind forcibly to the attention of the House and country i he would not be discharging the duty he owes to the people he was sent here to represent. I do not know that I need deal further with the statement which was made by my hon. friend the exMinister of Militia, and the very unsatisfactory statement made by the Minister of Finance, but just let me say this in passing, that it is a habit with hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, when fault is found with them, when it has been shown that they are wasting money, or distributing patronage for party purposes, at once to begin to talk about the bravery of our gallant boys at the front. As if the fact that upwards of 400,000 of Canadian boys have shown their willingness to shed their blood in defence of the Empire was a defence of the shortcomings of the Government ! But that is what they do. That is what my hon. friend the Minister of Finance has done to-day. Instead of answering the just criticisms made by the exMinister of Militia, he tells us what has been accomplished by our brave boys; he

tells of the sacrifices that are being made by the mothers, fathers and sisters of the boys who have gone to the front, as well a,s of the sacrifices which the boys themselves are making.
The Minister of Finance says we ought not to criticise the leadership which this Government has given the people. Well, I do not know that we are debarred from doing that, if we honestly think they might have done much better than they have done. If we honestly think they have mismanaged the affairs of this country since the war began, I do not think we ought to hesitate, I do not think we should be discharging our duty if we did hesitate to criticise the Government. But the Minister of Finance says: If you do not like our military leadership, see how splendidly we have led you in finance. See how splendidly we have led you in the way of borrowing money, and increasing the revenues and trade of this country. He even boasted of the fact that whereas some three years ago we only had a trade of between $500,000,000 and $600,000,000 in the current year our export and import trade will be in the vicinity of $2,000,000,000. Sir, I think that trade is not a trade for us to rejoice in. It is a trade that is washed in blood. It is a trade that tells many a tragic story of many a broken heart. It is a trade that is dependent entirely upon the war. We bring our imports of the comparatively raw materials from the United States; we manufacture them in our munitions factories and other factories throughout this country, and then send them forward as manufactured goods at. a higher valuation, which includes the labour that has been put upon them. That is how our present exports are largely made up.
What about profits?

And the profits which
have gone to the munition manufacturers are also counted in the value of the export. When the war is over matters will get down again to a normal condition, and these fictitious exports and imports will no longer be a factor in the prosperity of our country. Look at the'United States. Some politicians there are boasting of the enormous exports of the United States, but the right-thinking people of that country are pointing out that these exports are entirely fictitious and wholly due to the war, that they have grown to abnormal proportions, and have brought amazing wealth to the people of the United States. But the wealth comes from
a war in which they are taking no part. For us, this greatly increased wealth comes from a war in which we are taking a heroic, a noble, but at the same time, a sad part, and I, for one, would be very glad indeed to see the time come when these enormous exports would cease, and we would again have peace in Canada, peace in the Empire, and peace throughout the world.
I de-sire, with the indulgence of the House, to speak for a short time on a few matters which are contained in the speech from the Throne, as this is the only oppor-, tunity which one will have of referring to these questions which are general in character, but which at the same time are of considerable public interest. In his speech His Excellency makes this statement:
Steps have been taken by my advisers for better organization of National Service, and attention has been given to more thorough utilization of our natural resources.
This brings to my mind a subject which I think ought to have been dealt with long since by this Government. I am told by experts that we have in Canada natural resources, which, if they had been taken hold of in a proper manner, would have furnished the raw material for practically everything which is required by Canada for war purposes. Instead of spending in other countries vast sums of money for raw ma-[DOT] terial, we have plenty of raw material at hand, which might have been utilized. After two and a half years of war, we are told by the Government, what? That attention has been given to the more thorough utilization of our natural resources. Attention in what way? Have they appointed a commission to investigate? If they have, it will be about the 106th commission which this Government have appointed since they came into office. Perhaps my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen), who seems to be taking a serious view of the Observations which I have been making, will enlighten the House upon this subject, because it will be interesting to know in what respect this Government are paying attention to the natural resources of this country. What are they doing in the way of assisting in the development of out mining industry? What are they doing to encourage the utilization, within our own country, of the magnificent and valuable nickel deposits of Canada? What are they doing in the way of shipbuilding, of utilizing the vast deposits of iron for the purpose of building ships? In this, the third year of the war, the Government must confess that they have done absolutely nothing.

I trust my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries will pardon me for calling his attention to some of his political activities, as, of course, it is difficult to refrain from doing so, because my hon. friend is very much in the limelight. Not long ago he went to the province of Quebec in order to attend a very interesting ceremony at the Vickers Maxim dock of launching a dredge or an ice-breaker-I forget which it was, and he spoke there of the great work which is being done in shipbuilding in Canada. My hon. friend, however, did not tell the assembled guests-perhaps he had not time to do it-that they would not be building any ships in the Vickers Maxim plant had it not been for the course which the late Government pursued when I was Minister of Public Works. It was at that time and under our administration that the Vickers Maxim plant was established, which has enabled them to do the creditable work to which my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries referred. My hon. friend also spoke of the .splendid ships which were being built at the head of lake Superior by the Port Arthur Dock and Shipbuilding Company, which is not only building some splendid ships to sail on the Great Lakes, but which is now building some ships for the Norwegian Government. My hon. friend did not stop to think. If he had, perhaps he would have remembered that I turned the first sod of that dTy dock and shipbuilding plant at Port Arthur when I was Minister of Public Works, and it has been doing magnificent work since. My hon. friend would have probably had brought to his mind that uneasy thought which would perhaps have caused him some unihappiness, that not long ago he told the members of this House and the people in the country that it would take twenty-five years or on to fifty years to establish a 'shipbuilding yard in Canada. If he had paid especial attention to the Port Arthur Dry Dock and Shipbuilding Company, he would have known that it only took the short period of two or three years to get that plant into working condition so that it could turn out the greatest steamers that ever floated on the Great Lakes. So I could go on with other cases. But I wish that my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries had been able, on that pleasant and interesting occasion, to tell the people that the Government had taken steps to establish shipbuilding plants in the Maritime Provinces. I well remember that in one of those eloquent speeches which my hon.

friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries knows so well how to make speeches which thrill the hearts and evoke the admiration of his listeners, he told this House that he longed to see shipbuilding established in the Maritime Provinces; that he had the smell of the sea in his nostrils, and that he was simply aching to commence an enterprise of that character on behalf of the Government of this country.
He -must not forget this; and if he ever does, I shall be sure to remind him of it, because I do not want him ever to forget it; I do not want this Government ever to forget it, and I do not want the people, who wish to know what a great penalty has been paid by the people of Canada 'because of the unholy alliance between the Nationalists and the Conservative party in 1911, ever to forget it. Let me remind my hon. friend that when he came into the office of Minister of Marine and Fisheries in the fall of 1911, he found on the files of his department an offer from one of the greatest shipbuilding firms in the United Kingdom, the firm of Cammell, Laird and Company, agreeing to establish a magnificent shipbuilding yard at the port of St. John, to build ten war vessels, mamely, six cruisers and four destroyers, and to have them all completed before or in the year 1916, the year which is now-past. He also found there on deposit the sum of $100,000 as a guarantee that this great shipbuilding company would perform its contract. What did my hon. friend do? During the election of 1911, the Nationalist party of Quebec had declared that we should have no Canadian navy, that being a part of their policy. They were not going to participate in the wars of the Empire; they were not going to allow Canadians to man the ships of Canada to sail upon the high seas, and to have their young men disembowelled upon the seas of China, or of Europe; they would pledge themselves to secure the repea1 of the Naval Service Act, and there wa.- to be no Canadian navy. When my lit n. friend came into power, dearly as he would have liked to establish that shipbuilding plant at the port of St. John, dearly as he would have liked to enter into that contract with Cammell, Laird and Company, his hands and the hands of the other members of the Government were tied by that unholy alliance between the Liberal-Conservative party and the Nationalist party, which has been like a millstone around the necks of the peoplb

of Canada from that day to this. The Government did not dare go on because they were bound not to go on, and they returned the deposit to Cammell, Laird and Company, and the contract was never entered into. And that magnificent inlet of the Bay of Fundy at the port of St. John, where this splendid shipbuilding yard would have been built, had the contract been let by my hon. friend, according to the tender, where to-day there would have been ships under construction, where there would have been from three to five thousand men employed, where there would have been great docks, that splendid sheet <'! water to-day is as quiet as a grave. Where there would have been the hum of industry, to-day there is nothing but the sound of the seagulls passing over the waves. All is dead, as dead as this Government will be, when the people of Canada have an opportunity at the next election of expressing their will.

Did you hear
about Dorchester?

Yes, I heard about Dorchester, and let me tell my hon. friend what I heard about Dorehestef. My hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Blon-din) stated that all that he did with regard to the money which Allison took was to tell the people that they were not concerned because it was England's money and not Canada's money which had been taken, and that all that he told them with regard to conscription was to point out to them that Mr. Cannon had said there would be conscription, but that the young men of Ste. Rose need not mind it because, if they did not want to serve their country, they had a remedy, they could easily cross the border and seek safety in the United States.
In addition to that, I heard another thing that Mr. Sevigny said. He claimed credit, even now, for having prevented the building of a Canadian navy. That is quite in accordance with the position -which was taken by gentlemen like Mr. Blondin and Mr. Sevigny when a contribution of three battleships was suggested. They assured the people that that did not mean anything at all as compared with the proposal for the building of a Canadian navy. The building of ships would mean that Canadian boys would have to man them, but the giving of three dreadnoughts would simply mean that so much money, coming mostly out of the English-speaking people
of Ontario, 'would be contributed. This, they said their friends would not mind very much, because the money would be all they would have to contribute and their young men would remain safely at home.
Something was said by one ,of the hon. gentlemen who spoke in this debate with regard to the great mistake Canada had made in not giving three dreadnoughts to the Empire. Looking at matters in a practical way, I appeal to every right thinking member of this House-which is, I think, appealing to every member, because while we sometimes differ I am satisfied that we all try to think aright-as to whether it would not have been a splendid thing for Canada to-day if we had even the ten ships which were to be constructed under the Naval Act of 1910. Opportunities have not been wanting in which they could have done great service to the Empire and have added to the glory of Canada. Only the other day a Hun Taider appeared in the waters of the S.outh Atlantic, and within a few days from 16 to 20 merchant vessels were sent to the bottom. If we had those ten vessels for the protection of our trade routes, as was designed by the Government which was led hy the right hon. gentleman who now leads the Opposition, these vessels would be patrolling the north and south Atlantic looking for raiders and doing work which now has to be done by British ships. In this we would be following the splendid example which Australia has set in constructing a navy designed for the protection of her own coasts and available to the Empire in time of war. The war has now lasted more than two years, and we do not know how long it may continue. Even now it is not too late for my hon. friend., on the treasury benches to take hold of the question of building a Canadian navy. It may not yet be too late to build vessels to form part of a 'Candian navy-cruisers, destroyers and submarines-which would be of enormous benefit to Canada and to the Empire.
In the speech from the Throne there is another paragraph of great interest. It is as follows:
The life of the present Parliament will expire in October next, and under existing legislation a dissolution and election would be necessary in the early future. My advisers, however, are of opinion that the wishes of the Canadian people and the urgent requirements of the war would be best met by avoiding the distraction and confusion consequent upon a general election at so critical a time.
~ If it were possible to avoid a general election during the war, it would be desirable to do so, provided such a course

Many people throughout the country said to u.s last year: if you grant an extension, a precedent will be created; you may be asked to grant another, and it will be difficult for you to refuse. I think there was a good deal in the position taken by Mr. Lamarche, from the province of Quebec, who said that under the Constitution of Canada, Parliament has to sit for five years; that he was elected to serve the people for a term of five years and that he could not conscientiously vote himself a longer term as a member of Parliament. 10 p.m. tlemen on the other side will take occasion to let us know whether there is any truth in the rumour that the Minister of Public Works will accompany the Prime Minister to England and that when the date of re-assembling comes there will be no meeting, but a dissolution of Parliament and an appeal to the people. If that decision has been arrived at the House and the country ought to be taken into the confidence of the Government at as early a date as possible.
