speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: We might as well set my hon. friend's mind at rest at once. He can depend upon being called upon early in the spring to attend business as usual.

I am very glad to have that assurance from my hon. friend. He will observe that I am not nervous by reason of the rumour which I have heard. I believe in the words:
Still achieving, still pursuing,
Learn to labour and to wait.
Especially wait.

Whenever the elections come-and I am prepared to wait until they do come-I shall be ready to submit to any fate that may befall me.

My right hon. friend the Prime Minister is going to England to represent Canada as a temporary member of the War Cabinet. I assume that he will have the right to vote at the meetings of this conference. My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition took occasion early in the session to say that the Liberal members in the House would facilitate in every way the Prime Minister's attendance at that conference.
I am very glad, as one member of this House, that my right hon. friend made that statement, because, of course, it makes the path of the leader of the Government easier, and we shall all be prepared to make any sacrifice necessary in order to allow him so to attend. As one member of this House, I desire to say that when he goes to England he will have the sympathy and the support, I believe, of all the people of this country, irrespective of party, irrespective of their political differences, irrespective of the faults which we have to find with the Government in its administration in the past. We are all united in the one desire to serve the Empire in every possible way.
With regard to the conduct of the war, I am sure that he can carry to His Majesty the King and to the British Government a guarantee that the people of this country, irrespective of party, irrespective of religion or race, are united in a determination to make every sacrifice which is humanly possible in order to carry the war to success.
With regard to the terms of peace, of course we can say nothing. I notice that is one of the great subjects on which the overseas ministers are expected to deliberate.. But let me say to my right hon. friend that the people of this country, while praying for peace, yet want a peace with glory for the Empire, and a peace which we can be sure will be lasting, and which will secure the realization of those ideals for which the Empire and our Allies are fighting. We trust that when it comes the joy bells will ring around the world acclaiming a victory for democracy, for civilization and for the highest Christianity.

Unfavourable weather conditions and the scarcity of farm hands have left unproductive in 1916 part of the wheat fields of the West which were under crop in 1915, with this result that in the United States and Canada and the whole of North America the production of wheat has been from 500 to 600 millions of bushels short of that of the year 1915.

If I draw conclusions from the article I have just quoted and which seems to me well founded, the present Government should stimulate in every way the production of wheat, and not only in the Canadian West, touit also in all the provinces of the Dominion. I gave a few lectures last summer in the county of Masfcinonge, which I have the honour of representing in this House, and have advised the farmers to sow wheat. Some have followed this advice and are now quite satisfied, for you know that wheat is highly priced and flour is dear. I believe that by .sending lecturers through all the provinces-even in our province of Quebec-we would help not only our own Canadian population, tout also the Allies who are now fighting for the cause of civilization.

On motion of Hon. Mr. Hazen, it was ordered that this House do to-morrow resolve itself into a committee to consider of the ways and means for raising the Supply to be granted to His Majesty.

On motion of Hon. Mr. Hazen, the House adjourned at 10.20 p.m.
Wednesday, January 31, 1917.
